About this work

Liber de Triplici Regione Claustralium et Spirituali Exercitio Monachorum — "On the Threefold Region of Cloister-dwellers and the Spiritual Exercise of Monks" — is Trithemius's most systematic treatise on the monastic spiritual life. It divides the interior life of a cloistered monk into three stages — beginners (purification), proficients (illumination), and the perfect (union with God) — drawing the scheme from Pseudo-Dionysius and the Victorines and applying it to Benedictine observance. Completed in manuscript in 1497, it is one of the central texts of his Sponheim reform programme.

This is the 1516 Leipzig edition (BSB scan), a later reprint of the text first printed at Mainz in 1498. It is one of three witnesses of the De Triplici Regione in this corpus: the 1498 Mainz edition (prdl-24385), the 1498 e-rara witness (prdl-70285), and this 1516 Leipzig printing. The Latin was re-OCR'd from the page scans and translated by GPT-5.5. No published English translation is known;

    On the Threefold Region of Cloister-dwellers and the Spiritual Exercise of Monks

    Book on the Threefold Region of Cloistered Persons and on the Spiritual Exercise of Monks: no less useful than necessary for all religious.

    Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, revising the little work.

    Hermann Tulichus to the pious and religious brother, professor Christian [unclear].

    Ethereal Olympus yields to no one after death who passes the swift days without toil. Whatever in this life you say and do freely, an account must be rendered before God as witness. Not he who gives himself to Venus, to downy beds, and to devouring Ceres enjoys the starry heaven after his death. The man devoted to enticements is barred from the realm of the gods; the stars indeed must be sought by a narrow way. While, unharmed, we feed upon the living air of heaven, the kingdoms of the paradisal soil must be earned. After death we cast belated cries into the ether, lamenting that we have gone down into the Stygian pools. But because the strict Judge after our final fate pays no heed to complaints, now, lover of piety, the sentence after death must be considered with watchful mind: that rewards await each person according to his own merit. As soon as you ponder this with yourself in a thoughtful heart, if you yourself are wise, you will set a limit to sin.

    Do not sin; God sees.

    Letter of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, on the little work concerning the threefold region of cloistered persons.

    To the reverend fathers in Christ, the lord presidents, definitors, and the other abbots of the annual chapter of the Order of Saint Benedict, of the Bursfelde Union and Observance: Brother Johannes Trithemius, called abbot in Sponheim, of the same order and congregation, of the diocese of Mainz, sends reverence and charity.

    Most honored fathers, I have complied with your commands, and, as you instructed me, I undertook to correct the little work on the threefold region of cloistered persons, together with the spiritual exercise of monks, recently issued by the venerable father, lord Johannes, abbot of Bursfelde. And indeed, unless your authority had compelled me, I would never have dared to lay my hand upon the distinguished work of so great a father, who, it is agreed, being far more learned and holier than I, wrote most excellently. For what would I correct, where everything is found most approved? A good and devout man wrote no otherwise than he lived and than was fitting.

    Nevertheless, in order to satisfy both your command and the prayers of the author himself, I rendered the whole little work in briefer, though not fewer, sentences; and, attending to [unclear], I brought it, as far as I could, into my own manner and style of writing. But I kept the order and matter of the earlier volume; I completely changed the form and habit of expression. I added many things that seemed useful to me in almost every place; I removed a few; in individual passages I altered the words, not the sense. For both your command gave me warrant to dare this, and the insistent request of the aforesaid father persuaded me.

    For you wished that I should make a new work out of old material, should add whatever seemed suitable to me, should cut away superfluities, should alter [everything?] according to the powers of my talent, which are slight; this I completed by rewriting. Receive now, therefore, most beloved fathers, a work not mine but yours, not composed by me, but rather rewritten. If the labor of the aforesaid father pleases you, praise his talent; but if it displeases because of its meanness, correct my imperfection, since I, who had excellent material for spiritual building from another’s expenditure, have through my inexperience fashioned an unsuitable structure. If I have become a fool, you compelled me. Therefore, whether the work pleases or displeases, it is better for me, by writing ineptly, to have undertaken your command obediently than, contrary to obedience, to have held

    [unclear] silence. Yet I trust not in my own powers but in the merits of others, because a work which charity has brought forth will displease no lover of God.

    I pray that your Paternities may always remain blessed in Christ. From Spanheim, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of September, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1497.

    Hermannus Tulichus to the religious brothers of the order of Saint Benedict: greeting in the Lord.

    Everyone knows with how great care the ancient Romans, and other peoples alien to Christian piety, acted not only to preserve but also to enlarge their superstition, if he has merely handled the ancient monuments of that nation. Indeed, the slightest fault in religion, either insufficiently diligently observed or neglected through carelessness, they punished with great severity. Since this is so, with how great effort must you, professors of the Christian faith and religion, strive, not only to observe the worship of the true God, but also, according to your strength, equally to confirm and increase it?

    This is what the noble and most zealous defender of the Christian name and religion, Heinrich von Schleinitz, abbot in Chemnitz, and the most watchful propagator and champion of divine worship, Johannes Schreiger, abbot in Marienzell, carefully considering, procure all things which awaken and enlarge love for Jesus Christ, the vindicator of the human race from diabolical servitude. Of this matter, among many other things, this above all is evidence: that they are the chief authors in ensuring that, with the present little book copied in a thousand examples, the opportunity of reading it should be available to all those who, according to their profession, wish to exercise themselves in Christian piety.

    Therefore all who wish both to be called Christians and to be regarded as such, and especially the brothers who have entered the religion of Saint Benedict, must strive that you not merely read through this little book often, but constantly exercise yourselves in those things which are most holily prescribed in it. This is certainly worth the labor, provided that after death you are to go happily into the kingdom of heaven, which, as it is in the sacred writings, suffers violence and the violent seize it. Let us strive earnestly and with all, as they say, our strength, that through the grace of God, best and greatest, we may all be led after death from this valley of tears to that place. Farewell. Given at Leipzig, in the house of Melchior Lotter, in the year from the reconciled divinity 1516.

    Here begins the book on the threefold region of cloistered persons, and on the spiritual exercise of novices.

    When I recall to mind the state of monastic life in this time, I grieve deeply over its calamity, because the fervor of spiritual exercise which once produced very abundant fruits in the order of our holy father Benedict has now, for the most part, departed from monks. For we see cloistered persons returning in their morals to the world; we see the institution of regular observance despised by many; and religion, which at the beginning had been instituted for contempt of the world, is again recalled to the pomp of the world through wicked monks.

    The crown of our head has fallen; the integrity of regular discipline has been corrupted, and the former fervor of conduct has perished. We see very many monasteries of our order lying buried in the worst deformity; very few do we see reformed to the purity of the Rule. But the cause of this fall of regular institution is negligence of spiritual exercises, because as soon as the spirit of fervor in the minds of cloistered persons lost its savor, the flesh, previously dead through denial of itself, revived, and the world, which before had appeared dry and hopeless to devout hearts, began again to flourish in carnal minds.

    For truly the thought of the human heart, inclined to evil from youth, unless it has been daily stirred to fervor of spirit by the bridle of spiritual exercise, soon falling back into its former negligences, grows lukewarm from its holy purpose. For just as newly broken land, deprived of the diligent care of the cultivator, with thorns growing up, quickly returns into the solitude of its former state, so the human mind, however pure or holy it may be, is quickly reduced to the brambles of vices unless it is renewed to fervor of spirit by the daily exercise of devotion.

    Led by this consideration, the fathers of our Bursfeld observance, devout cultivators, entrusted to us and to posterity by word and example that we, who for our frailty cannot remain constant in fervor of spirit, should at least by evening recollection after compline, accusing our daily negligences, renew the state of our mind to the fervor of our holy purpose. But whoever has neglected the daily exercise of this institution falls into the depth of torpor, just as the wise man says in Ecclesiasticus: “If you do not hold yourself steadfastly in the fear of the Lord, your house will quickly be overthrown”; by this is understood good confidence. For this exercise, so useful and so necessary

    [unclear] provision, the Rule of our most holy father Benedict seems to suffice for the monk, since it is agreed that it contains all the material of the exercises, both spiritual and bodily, necessary for monks for the preservation of regular discipline. And therefore all the exercises of monks are to be humbly submitted to the constitutions of the Rule, since whatever is prescribed either by us or by others for the instruction of monks is wholly directed to the observance of the monastic norm. For the sum of our whole religious life, which is acquired by the continuance of spiritual exercise, is contained in compendium in the Rule of monastic tradition, as in a root. Therefore every exercise of monks, whether spiritual or bodily, by which the mind is brought through love to humble obedience and self-denial, is conformed to the institutions of the holy Rule; the more it is recognized as presenting a good and humble monk as near to God, by so much the more it opposes the pursuits of the proud contemner. The holy mysteries of this exercise direct the mind of its cultivator, by an invisible teaching, toward the love of God, as toward its due end, along a secure path; they wonderfully acquire the grace of inward devotion, and make the monk despise all earthly things as nothing, and sweetly burn at all times in fervor of spirit. The animal man does not perceive this salutary exercise of devotion; the vain and curious monk does not understand this pursuit; the proud man does not admit this knowledge, which is to be preferred to all things. Happy is he who has learned to penetrate the secrets of this exercise; happy is he who has deserved to receive from the Lord this gift of holy compunction, which, once anyone has perfectly obtained it, he will fear no adversities of this world. But that exercise which, lacking its due end, does not direct the minds of cloistered men to the observance of the commandments of the Rule, the holy Spirit of discipline does not infuse, since where the obedience of subjection is despised, no gift is accepted by almighty God. For it is written: Obedience is better than victims, and to hearken rather than to offer fat. And although many little works of spiritual exercise composed by various authors are found, yet, because not all things suit all people, it has seemed good also to you to publish something in accordance with the Rule of our most holy father Benedict, by which we may more greatly and more nearly stir ourselves to the purity of regular observance. Accordingly, we divide the present little work, collected from the exercises of the excellent father Theodoric the abbot, into two principal parts: the first of which is set forth in consideration of monastic instruction; the second is occupied with the exercise of the spiritual life. In the first te

    you are bidden to know him; in the second, to raise the mind from earthly things to heavenly. Therefore, approaching as best we can the subject proposed for our consideration, we divide the first treatise into three parts, according to the threefold state of cloistered men, of whom we may call the first sensual, the second rational, the third spiritual. From this threefold state of men we take a fitting title for this work, which we call On the Threefold Region of Cloistered Men. In these three regions the whole multitude of monks is comprised, as will be said in what follows.

    On the first region of the soul, in which carnal monks live with beasts: disordered by many passions, living sensually in the lowest region

    The first region of the soul, then, is called sensual, lowest, and also animal; in it the roots of all evils are contained. Men placed in this dark region share, in their kind, with beasts, since they observe, so to speak, bestial habits, while they give either nothing or little to reason, but, like beasts, yield everything to sensuality. For in that lowest region three sensual powers of the soul preside: the first, the sensitive power, is spread about the objects of the five senses; the second, the concupiscible power, delights in carnal things; the third, the irascible power, flees things contrary to the pleasures of the flesh.

    And this lowest region is compared to the airy heaven, because, just as hailstorms, snows, lightning, and various tempests are generated in the air, so too in the minds of carnal men inhabiting this dark region various tempests of vices rage. Woe to carnal monks who inhabit this dark region, in which the motion of crimes is frequent and the storm of pleasures continual. These are monks given over to animal passions, who subject reason to sensuality, who live according to the flesh in bestial desires. Manifest, moreover, are the works of the flesh among those dwelling in this lowest region: fornication, uncleanness, shamelessness, luxury, service of idols, sorceries, enmities, rivalries, angers, quarrels, dissensions, sects, envies, murders, drunkenness, feasting, and things similar to these. Concerning them the apostle cries out directly that those who do such things will not obtain the kingdom of God. These are those living in the lowest work of religion, who despise the traditions of the holy fathers, who presumptuously contemn the precepts handed down by their elders. These are the unclean worshippers of the lowest region, given over to vices and carnal desires, who do not care to have God in their knowledge, who serve the pleasures of the flesh, who [unclear] the vow of holy religion which they have professed, who, despising the salvation of their souls, scorn to follow the grace of God calling them.

    Therefore he handed them over to a reprobate sense and to false judgment, so that they judge evil to be good, and falsely suppose that the things which in truth are worst are themselves best. These are those of whom the holy apostle prophesied: carnal monks, whisperers, detractors, hateful to God, insulting, proud, puffed up, inventors of evils, disobedient to superiors, foolish, disorderly, without affection, without covenant, without mercy, filled with every iniquity, malice, wickedness, contention, deceit, and malignity; although they know the justice of God, they do not wish to understand that those who do such things are worthy of eternal death, and not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those who do them, and those who by duty of office by no means oppose the pursuits of the wicked. For indeed the ruler of souls who does not correct his offending subjects involves himself in damnation for the crimes of others, and by keeping silent becomes their associate, whose faults condemnation will follow. For whoever is appointed shepherd of souls and neglects to correct sinners according to the canonical rule, even if he is free of his own offense, nevertheless will be condemned before the strict judge for another’s merit.

    For the supreme shepherd says to the prophet: Son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel, and you shall hear the word from my mouth, and you shall announce it to them from me. If, therefore, when I say to the wicked man, You shall surely die, you have not announced it to him, nor have spoken so that he may turn away from his wicked way and live, then that wicked man indeed shall die in his iniquity, but I will require his blood from your hand. And Benedict our father says in the Rule: Let the abbot know that the fault lies upon the shepherd if he shall have been able to find anything of less profit for the father of the household in his sheep. O sentence always to be feared by all shepherds: because not only is the depraved conduct of subjects ascribed to the ruler, but he is also held guilty before the inward judge for their lesser progress. O what shall we wretched shepherds say in that strict examination, we who neglect to correct according to the Rule the monks entrusted to us when they offend in many ways; who do not call those lying in the lowest region to higher things, but, carnal with the carnal, grow numb in the shadow of death with harmful idleness. Woe to all who remain in this dark region, because unless they do penance, they must be assigned with those who [unclear] darkness

    they dwell in the outer [places], where no order dwells, but perpetual horror. For just as monks who, according to the Rule, walk in the spirit are to be happily crowned without end in heaven with the holy angels, so, conversely, those who, contrary to the norm of monastic institution, persevere in the flesh in this lowest region even unto death, being worse than pagans, are to be tortured eternally in hell with the demons. For that blessed man truly said: “As I have never seen better men than those who have made progress in the cenobium, so I have not found worse men than those who have failed in the monastery.”

    For the monastic profession requires the perfection of the spiritual life, and tends toward the summit of the virtues as toward its proper due end. But by however much anyone, placed in the monastery, has fallen away from this effort of making progress, by so much the farther does he withdraw from the purpose of a monk.

    In what manner the carnal monks, citizens of this lowest region, are disordered in many articles.

    Although the description of this lowest region applies generally to all carnal men who dwell with beasts in sins and crimes, nevertheless, so that we may attend to our own affairs, we intend to speak of lukewarm and carnal cloistered men, doing no injury at all to the good and devout. For always and in all things we wish the conduct of good cloistered men to remain untouched and unharmed whenever we discuss the evil pursuits of the wicked. Thus we rebuke evil cloistered men and depraved conduct; honoring the good, we praise them everywhere, as is fitting. And what else than evil can we say about the evil, in whom we find no good things to say? In a holy order they live disorderly lives; they despise the traditions of the elders; they do not admit words of salvation. Indeed, the disorder of the monks of the lowest region is so great that, in my judgment, it would be easier to convert a publican than to recall a disordered monk to repentance. We comprise this disorder of carnal monks in eight articles, although we are not unaware that they are disordered in many other things.

    And first, indeed, the citizens of this lowest region, beastly monks, are disordered toward God; then toward their own prelate; third, the prelate toward his subjects; fourth, the members toward one another; again, fifth, they are disordered toward themselves; then toward the property of the monastery; seventh, toward contempt of the world; consequently, toward repentance for sin. These are the principal disorders of the citizens of the lowest region; these are the beastly dispositions of carnal monks, who dwell in the lowest things in mind and body, who do not hasten to make progress toward the summit. Therefore, to set out briefly, in order, these disordered conditions of the lowest region, and to show, as far as we can, how far carnal monks are from God. For, as the Prophet says, salvation is far from sinners.

    In what manner the carnal monks, citizens of this lowest region, are disordered in many articles.

    In what way the citizens of this lowest region are disordered toward God. Article I.

    Therefore the carnal monks of this lowest region, mad worshippers, are in many ways disordered toward God; they never feel the sweetness of his love; they admit no compunction of divine fear; in their affections they are beastly and swollen with pride; in their carnal pleasures they are at all times unclean. And first, indeed, their disorder toward God takes its origin from ignorance: for, being given over to animal passions, they do not care to have God in their knowledge, nor do they consent to ponder in their mind those things that lead to fear of him. But, blinded by evil desires, they become vain in their thoughts. But what does Scripture say? “He who is ignorant shall be ignored.” They do not wish to understand, that they may do well; they do not tremble before the face of the strict judge; without repentance they continually persevere in evils.

    Indeed, like beasts of burden, they do not fear to rot away in their pleasures; they pay no heed to the patience of God calling them to repentance; they seek nothing other than the comforts of their flesh. At all times they walk in the greatest sins without any fear; they stubbornly refuse to know the ways of the Lord. Of the future judgment they think either nothing or little; they do not fear the punishments prepared in hell for sinners; the grace of compunction never pierces their hearts, whose mind the love of God does not inflame. They have no care for God; no dread of death. They obey the belly rather than God; they desire at all times to live according to the flesh; and while they shamefully neglect their own salvation, they descend to hell with the demons. Indeed, those who, forgetful of God, keep badly the vow of holy monastic conduct do not attain to the heavenly rewards of life to be bestowed upon the just.

    Secondly, carnal monks are disordered toward God through foolish profession, because they promise to live according to the Rule, yet they do not truly care to fulfill this. And what is more disordered than to promise to the Lord God strictness of life, and to remain in the foulness of one’s former life? He is a mocker of almighty God, not a monk, whoever lives in a monastery otherwise than the monastic Rule teaches. O how many today do we see living secularly within the cloister; how many do we see neglecting the purpose of their profession; who violate the observance of regular discipline in various ways; who knowingly ignore the goodness of God; who refuse to do penance.

    Thirdly, many cloistered men of this lowest region are disordered toward God through neglect of the service owed to him: they serve their own affections and carnal desires in various ways, and with a distracted mind approach the service of God. Of these, some hasten to choir without any devotion

    are lukewarm. Others, compelled by necessity, come unwillingly; certain ones, scattered by outward thoughts, are present at divine services in body, but outside they wander in mind through various workshops. Others do not fear to seek false occasions by which they may, as if licitly, be able to absent themselves from choir. Now they feign a severe headache; now they mendaciously allege this, now that; and while they deceitfully withdraw the service owed to almighty God, they incur the reproach of eternal malediction owed to the negligent.

    Fourth, there are many who are disordered toward God by the working of habit: although they may at times be free from the malediction of the negligent, they nevertheless never approach the fruit of inward devotion. For they come to the service of God from habit alone, nor are they moved to any good work by devotion. Others, placed under grave necessity, obey the commands of superiors quite unwillingly, and fear temporal punishments more than the judgment of God. These bear the cross of the Lord with Simon under compulsion; like the heifer of Ephraim led to the threshing-floor, they apply themselves to good works by habit alone. But those who come to the service of God with an intention that is not due do a good thing not well. They also perform the deed of a just man without the reward of a just man, who in good works do not also take on the good will of a just man.

    Fifth, the citizens of the lowest region are disordered toward God through the vice of ingratitude, which is the greatest crime of a disordered will. And indeed, one who is found ungrateful to the Lord for benefits received is often exposed, by his own demerit, to be scourged by various and most grievous temptations. And therefore he deserves to lose the benefit that he has received, because he neglects to show himself grateful to so great a benefactor. And what greater ingratitude can there be than to live irreligiously in religion, to break a vow, and shamefully to violate a resolution solemnly undertaken? For a monk who entangles himself in carnal vices, who neglects to live according to the rule that he has professed, voluntarily incurs the greatest vice of ingratitude.

    In what manner the monks of this lowest region are disordered toward their prelate. Article II.

    Toward their prelate, carnal monks are disordered in many ways: they tear him apart with continual detractions; with a contumacious heart they disparage the pastoral office; they refuse to show their pastor the affection of filial love according to the rule. For, blinded by various pleasures of the flesh, the monks of this lowest region disdain to consider whose place the abbot holds in the monastery; and the one whom they should humbly venerate as Christ’s vicar, they think, as being like themselves by reason of infirmity, worthy of no honor. Beneath the snare of this disordered way of life, the ancient enemy deceives carnal monks, whom he leads in various ways into displeasure with their pastor.

    For the greatest power of raging against the monastic flock is granted to the devil when the one who presides is hated by his subjects. For just as a sick man who hates the physician and does not allow him to come near cannot be healed, so a monk who, because of aversion, does not wish to disclose his temptations to his pastor cannot be saved. For how will a sick sheep be able to escape the teeth of the ravening wolf, if it cannot endure the presence of the shepherd? First, therefore, disordered monks disparage the life of their pastor, and contumaciously accuse both his deeds and his words, because, when they see their ruler proceeding according to the traditions of the holy fathers, they fear being corrected in their own depravity. For among reprobate minds the life of the good is always drawn into suspicion; envy is always tormented by the virtues of others; and the monk who voluntarily subjects himself to vices and sins always hates a pastor of purified conduct.

    Secondly, the citizens of this shadowy region are disordered toward their prelate when his office is disparaged, though they do not fail to know that he was ordained by God to preside in the monastery. They murmur against him on slight occasion; his commands are not observed; and those who long ago had subjected themselves, for the love of God, with the arms of holy obedience, now, after obedience has been despised, in the manner of Sarabaites usurp for themselves the pernicious rule of their own wills. They desire to have an abbot suited to their own depraved morals. They reject one who is holy and useful. If they find a lax and sluggish pastor, they intoxicate him by flattery with many poisons; they call him the best and most pious father, and subject themselves to him not humbly but gladly, because from him they fear no correction of their depravity.

    Thirdly, carnal monks show themselves disorderly toward their pastors, when they withdraw themselves from them in the affection of filial love and scorn to obey according to the Rule. Yet since a monk is bound to love his abbot with sincere affection as the vicar of Christ, he will not be able to hate him without a most grievous crime. For indeed, he who does not love his pastor for the love of Christ is not a true lover of God. For how would Christ, who wishes even enemies to be loved, permit his own vicars to be hated? Therefore look to him who wished the abbot to be set over you in his place, and henceforth there will be no cause of displeasure against him.

    Fourthly, the disorderly citizens of the shady valley detract from the reverence due to their pastor, when they not only scorn to pay him the honor owed by the Rule, but, what is worse, do not fear even to inflict insult upon him. For the Rule states that the abbot bears the place of Christ in the monastery, to whom all monks ought humbly to obey as to Christ himself, since the obedience that is paid to superiors is shown to Christ. But perverse cloisterers, always ungrateful for the presidency of prelates, do not fear stubbornly to oppose the divine ordinance; they scorn to obey the commands of the holy Rule; and they dishonor their abbot, to whom they ought to have shown every reverence, tearing him with hatred and detractions. Whatever he has done, whatever he has said, displeases them as though badly done, since they detract at all times from his conduct and, despising his office, these diseased sheep seek nothing more than the confusion of their pastor. Some of them, judging their abbot in secret, despise him; others contradict him to his face. And while they neglect to show reverence to their pastor, they confound every observance of discipline. Pride is always familiar to these men, and the foulness of the flesh, because those who voluntarily withdraw themselves from the affection of their pastor fall into abominable temptations and the worst crimes. For whoever despises Christ’s vicar in the monastery hands over to the devil the power of raging against him, and confounds the union of the mystical body.

    Fifthly, carnal and disorderly monks detract from the authority of their pastor, when they think that nothing is permitted to him in the monastery unless they themselves have consented to it. With uplifted neck they despise the virtue of humility; they spurn regular subjection; they scorn to yield to their betters. They wish to thrust themselves into divine affairs and causes, and to usurp for themselves the primacy of counsel, so that the abbot dares to do or arrange nothing unless the business first proceeds with their consent. But what does the blessed lawgiver say in the Rule? “The abbot,” he says, “hearing the counsels of the brothers, should consider the matter within himself, and do what he judges more useful.” And again: “Let the brothers give counsel with all humble subjection, so that they do not presume stubbornly to defend what has seemed good to them; rather, let it depend on the abbot’s judgment, so that all may obey what he has judged to be more salutary.” And again, concerning the appointment of a prior, he says: “We judge it expedient, for the preservation of charity and peace, that the ordering of his monastery depend on the abbot’s judgment.” This ordering certainly concerns the appointment and removal of all officials of the monastery; it requires not the consent of the brothers, but the counsel of those who fear God. Finally, the Rule commands all things to be done according to the will of the abbot, and that absolutely nothing be presumed which has not been enjoined by him. Carnal monks, rash usurpers of their own will, try in various ways to weaken this authority of his and to disturb the order and charity of the whole monastery, when they think that the rector should do nothing except what they themselves think right. But tell me, proud cultivators of [unclear], who always establish your own will, who vo

    You usurp another's right for yourselves. Is this the virtue of obedience: to be unwilling to yield to the command of a superior, but stubbornly to cling to one’s own judgment? The holy father did not lay down in the Rule that you should live in this way, since he ordered you in all things to follow the will of the abbot. For obedience is the greatest virtue of a monk, which our divine father wished to commend so highly that he said that a good work done without the abbot’s will lacks merit. Hence, giving instruction, he concludes thus: “Therefore let all things be done with the abbot’s will, and let no one in the monastery follow his own will.” But if a discretion sufficient for the ordering of the monastery does not appear to be present in the ruler, that must be imputed to carnal monks, who voluntarily set over themselves one who was not suitable. Folly always hates prudence, and wicked monks detest a wise abbot. Therefore those who knowingly set a fool over themselves will necessarily be subject to his ordering and will. Indeed, no incapacity of the pastor ought to extinguish the obedience of subjects, since the Rule commands us to obey even an unprofitable one. For it says: “The precepts of the abbot are to be obeyed in all things, even if he himself, which God forbid, acts otherwise.” But carnal monks, reproving us for disobedience, object: “We do these things rightly and with a good intention, because we see the substance of the monastery perishing through bad government.” But the apostle contradicts you, since evils are not to be done so that good things may come, nor on account of the loss of a temporal thing is the subjection of humility to be abandoned. For where, between loss of temporal substance and danger to regular obedience, something must be undergone, it is better that the substance perish than that the purity of obedience be harmed. For God will not require money from our hands, but souls. Truly, he who is a true monk prefers the virtue of obedience to all the things of the world. But the citizens of this lowest region, carnal monks, tear apart the virtue of obedience in various ways; they attack the weapons of holy humility, so that it seems easier to me to establish a new monk from the world than to be able to amend the sloth of those men. But from their fruits we clearly know what sort they are, namely those who violate peace and charity in the monastery, disturb the concord of unity, sow discord between the brothers and the abbot, and stubbornly refuse to obey the commands of the Rule. These are the works of evil cloisterers; these are the marks of the citizens of the lowest region, since, as most wicked defenders of their own will, they cast aside the weapons of holy obedience; they live according to the flesh, not the spirit; they show either no deference or little to the statutes of the fathers; they do not acquiesce in sound counsels. Their damnation is just. For just as it is impossible for a blazing fire not to ascend upward, so it is not possible for a monk without obedience to penetrate the secrets of heaven.

    In what way the pastors of this lowest region are disordered toward their subjects. Article III.

    Since, however, we have shown that very many monks of the lowest region are disordered, and likewise their pastors, shall we not also show the disorders of prelates toward their subjects, as though sparing ourselves? Neither does the name of abbot sanctify anyone, nor does the preeminence of pastoral care save the undeserving. Therefore, since many among the prelates inhabit the mountain of the lowest region with the beasts of the earth, they must by no means be passed over by us in silence. For very many rulers of cloistered persons show themselves disordered toward their subjects: they not only neglect to feed according to the rule the souls committed to them, but tear and kill them in various ways. But whenever someone from the lowest region is taken up as a pastor, the pursuits of the wicked are strengthened for the worse. Therefore a good man, one who loves God, is to be promoted as abbot: one who has long since overcome this lowest region; one who has learned to subdue the passions of the flesh; one who both wishes and is able to ascend to that highest region of the spirit. For the abbot of monks must be of higher merit than the monks, since whoever is appointed ruler of souls must necessarily be adorned with many virtues. For if a weak pastor still dwells in the lowest region with the sheep, he kills the feeble by neglecting them; he does not strengthen them. For if a blind man offers guidance to a blind man, he must necessarily fall with him into the pit. But the pastor who does not show himself well ordered toward his subjects according to the rule is to be called not a pastor but a hireling, and he will not remain in the house of the Lord forever.

    Many, moreover, are the disorders of carnal prelates, which do harm so much the more widely as they are corrected the more rarely.

    And first, indeed, a ruler is disordered toward his subjects if he has been a hireling: if, with the sheep neglected, he seeks his own advantage of flesh or soul; if, so that he may be able to obtain his own will, he denies nothing contrary to the rule to those who ask. For truly the one who is a hireling does not truly love the sheep: he seeks his own glory, desires to be over others, does not care to be of service according to the rule, rejoices to be called abbot, does not know how to show himself a pastor. Therefore he receives the empty reward of his vanity: he who seeks not God's glory but his own; who would more readily permit the souls of his subjects to perish than resign the abbacy to another, better man. He is a hireling, and the sheep do not belong to him. He is not a true monk; he is not a good pastor; he is not a sincere lover of God, who, presiding over monks, is unwilling to step down if, by the counsel of those who fear God, it should seem expedient to do so. The care of governing souls despises the proud man; it requires one humble and resigned to God in all things. Therefore, if you wish to be found a good pastor and a true monk, remember that your intention must be formed in this way at all times: that you be ready, out of love for God, humbly to feed, according to your strength, the souls committed to you; that you also be ready to resign the pastoral office, at the judgment of God and of good men, from integrity of heart. If you have kept this intention always abiding in your mind, you will be a good pastor both to yourself and to others

    you will be. But if in pastoral care you love your own honor; if you prefer your own advantage to the benefit of your subjects, you still dwell with the beasts in the lowest region, and you show how disordered of heart you are.

    Secondly, the pastor of souls is rendered disordered toward his subjects if his mind is occupied too greedily with temporal affairs, if he bears greater anxiety for secular business than for the souls committed to him. This excessive care for temporal things holy father Benedict forbids in the Rule, and rightly judges rational souls to be preferred to all things of the world.

    “Before all things,” he says, “let the abbot not, by dissembling or making little of the salvation of the souls committed to him, bear more anxiety for transitory, earthly, and perishable things; but let him always consider that he has undertaken to govern souls, for which he will also render account.” Consequently the pious father assures him concerning the necessities of the body, if, loving God, he worships him with a pure mind. “And lest perhaps,” he says, “he complain of scantier substance, let him remember what is written: ‘Seek first the kingdom of God and his justice, and all these things shall be added to you.’ And again: ‘Nothing is lacking to those who fear God.’”

    But the disordered pastor of monks is led astray by the spirit of avarice; blinded in mind as though without feeling, he casts away from himself the fear of the Lord; sold under sin with Ahab, he runs to the aid of wickedness; he lacks confidence in the promises made through the holy father concerning the attainment of necessities; he is occupied with external matters more than befits a monk. Driven now thereafter by the goads of avarice, he despises the commands of God and of holy mother Church; he does not keep feast days; he plunges wholly into earthly affairs; he thinks on nothing but temporal things; he detests the observance of regular discipline; and when he fears being restrained from evil pursuits by the authority of the Chapter, he seeks the dissolution of the holy union.

    Then, having become reprobate with Saul, he calls upon the counsel of the pythoness; he declares the obedience of reform damnable for his monastery; he desires to be released [as quickly as possible?] from submission to the confederation; to this end he relates many things falsely and mendaciously. But when the authority of the annual Chapter is despised with impunity, it remains that monastic observance suffer shipwreck; for love of God keeps the good regularly in discipline, and fear of correction restrains the depraved from evil works. Whoever strives to evade the unity of the Chapter imitates the devil.

    Thus the emperor of the Bulgars forbids the Christians subject to him to hold an assembly in church, under penalty of death, yet grants them license to believe whatever they wish. For the cunning man knew that the sincerity of the Christian faith could not long endure, if it should happen

    the public office of exhortation to be lacking. This enemy of the Christian faith the disordered and carnal abbot strives, as far as he can, to imitate: he resists the commands of so necessary a chapter. For the authority of the chapter alone is what maintains the observance of regular discipline in the order; if it is despised, no integrity of monastic life will remain. But the disordered abbot, a dweller in the lowest region, invents innumerable reasons against regular observance; he falsely alleges that the conditions of his monastery are contrary; he complains that ancient privileges are being suppressed. He disdains that his monastery be subjected to anyone. But woe to disordered men, through whom even one monastery should happen to be lost from this most holy congregation.

    Finally, this plague of avarice makes an abbot not only disordered toward his subjects, but also contrary to himself and utterly turned away from God. For covetousness is the root of all evils; when it seizes a servant of Christ, it makes him a minister of the devil. Therefore the abbot who has subjected his mind to this vice shows himself to be not a shepherd but a hireling. He is always gaping after earthly profits; he cares nothing for the advancement of souls; a book of sacred reading is rarely or never seen in his hands; registers of rents are turned over more often. He joins field to field; he is always carrying together gold and silver to be buried in a chest; and while he desires too much that his monastery abound in temporal goods, he prepares prey for plunderers. For frequently the treasury of temporal lordship devours the monies of monasteries, which the excessive greed of monks brings into monasteries. Woe to you, avaricious shepherd of cloistered men, who bear greater anxiety for brute animals than for the souls committed to you. The horse grows sick and at once you prepare a remedy; a soul perishes and you think no danger threatens. The ox and the ass fall ill and you suffer with them; a brother is swallowed up by sadness and you do not come to his aid. You, therefore, hireling and not shepherd, who with a stubborn heart despise the infirmities of your brothers, who do not aid those set in bitterness, do not presume that you can escape the hand of the Lord, whose sheep you permit so wickedly to perish.

    The third way a ruler is disordered toward his subjects is when those whom he ought carefully to have kept within the enclosures of the monastery he places outside, not without danger. For indeed, when a weak cenobite is exposed to the rule of nuns or to secular churches, the integrity of regular observance is violated; because he who, still remaining in the lowest region, has not learned to subject the flesh to the spirit, does not know how to preside over others without danger to himself. But the disordered shepherd who, on account of the advantage of temporal property, does not fear to expose his monks to so great a danger, is guilty of all the souls perishing by such an occasion, and before the inward judge is bound to make restitution for all. It is not part of the profession of a monk to rule secular churches; it is not expedient for a weak man to preside over convents of nuns. But what? Therefore should a monk [unclear] oppose himself to the command of the shepherd, if

    ...has wished to reside with nuns or in churches of secular clergy? For the Rule commands that nothing is to be preferred to obedience. I truly do not know what I should answer to this question, so that I may not incur the danger which is seen to threaten on both sides. For if I tell the truth, I shall seem to violate the obedience of subjection; if I consent that monks are to be exposed to danger, I confess that I sin. Yet I shall say briefly what I think, although I am not unaware that the truth will give birth to hatred. Just as a monk, by the necessity of his profession, is bound simply to obey his pastor in all things that are according to the monastic Rule, so a prelate cannot compel a monk, without that monk’s own will, to things that are beyond the Rule, especially when danger to salvation intervenes. But to govern churches, to preside over women, to reside outside the monastery, is not according to the Rule [unclear]. Do not be angry with me, fathers, if I have spoken the truth; do not knit your brows if I have expressed what seems so to me. Nevertheless, you will do what seems good to you, even if I protest. But I beg you, do not expose your monks to danger to chastity; do not violently compel anyone to the governance of nuns and of parish churches, since you can find many who ambitiously seek these offices. Obedience is indeed good, but it must by no means be preferred to truth and the salvation of the soul. For when danger to salvation is at issue, it is better humbly to set obedience aside by making excuse than to suffer shipwreck of chastity. Woe to the prelates of monks who incorporate churches of secular clergy into their monasteries, who loosen their bosom to covetous desires by the torches of avarice, because, while they think they are doing good for posterity, they damn many through the occasion.

    Fourth, the governance of monks becomes disordered toward its subjects if it is found turbulent and anxious. In a pastor of souls a pious and prudent discretion is very necessary, lest either zeal, with discretion lacking, be excessive, or the measure of compassion be slackened by excessive laxity. But a disordered rector sometimes, through indiscreet fury, presents himself as a tyrant to the monks; sometimes, through a fixed compassion, he grows, as it were, insensible to the gravest crimes. He does not know the just moderation of governance; he does not experience in himself the warmth of brotherly charity; he always thinks himself lord of the monks; he does not know how to be the father and companion of the humble. What is more savage than this governance? What more wicked than this power, where God, reason, and understanding do not govern the impious man? The judgments of those presiding do not depart from the rectitude of the law of nature. A disordered and anxious rector is infected by beastly passions of various kinds; he always suspects evil of the monks; and while he directs the manner of governance [unclear], anxious, he always fears with Herod that he will lose his kingdom.

    Fifth, the pastor of cloistered men is said to be disordered toward the monks if, in distributing the goods of the monastery, he is held to be either excessive or obstinate. Excessive or...

    is to be called [such] if, in distributing, he has been wasteful, or extravagant with indiscriminate largess. But he is called obstinate if he has not given opportunely what ought to be given, or stubbornly withholds necessities from his subjects. He is also to be called obstinate who casts aside the fear of the Lord, who trusts too much in his own judgment, who in any matters to be done admits no counsels of the wise. And indeed among pastors of souls there are very many disordered by this sickness of mind, who either spend the property of the monastery too improvidently or preserve it with excessive tenacity. They prepare very sumptuous banquets for their flatterers, but to others, from whom they are averse, they deny even the smallest things.

    In the guest-house, or in their own abbey, pastors depraved by disordered conduct sometimes eat to the point of drunken excess; they always drink the best wine. But to poor monks, who by watching and singing bear the burden of the day and the heat, they grant necessary things scarcely and meagerly.

    Sixth, a prelate of monks is shown to be very disordered if, bold against God, he is lifted up into pride by making light of his judgments. For since a pastor cannot be corrected by his subjects, he is referred by the holy father Benedict to the judgment of God, as is found in many places of the Rule. “Let the abbot know,” he says, “that for all his judgments he must render account to God.” And again: “Let the ordained abbot always consider what sort of burden he has taken up, and to whom he is to render account of his stewardship.” And again he says: “As soon as faults begin to arise, let him cut them off with charity, not with tyranny.” And in another place he warns, saying: “Let the abbot himself, however, do all things with the fear of God and observance of the holy Rule, knowing beyond doubt that he will render account for all his judgments to God, the most just judge.”

    But the disordered ruler of monks, like an asp with stopped ears, despises hearing this threat of the most holy lawgiver; he scorns the patient long-suffering of God; he thinks nothing of the examination to come, until at last the most holy lawgiver, angered, says to him: “Restore to me without delay the souls once committed to you in the body. Return their number whole; for if even one of them has perished through your negligence, your soul shall not see my face forever.” What then will you answer to the highest pastor, useless ruler, when not only the blood of those perishing is required from you, but also an account of those making too little progress is demanded? Behold, now you walk in the worst security, despising the examination of God; you think that all things that please you in the body are lawful for you, and you do not think to whom you are one day to render account for all things. Soon the Lord of all will come, before whom you do not fear to show yourself an unfaithful servant, and whose honor you do not fear to arrogate to yourself. Unless meanwhile you do penance, unless you amend your life for the better, you will burn without end with the demons in hell.

    Seventh, it happens that a pastor is disordered toward his subjects if

    having neglected the common good, he has sought his own advantage with a vicious intention: if, presiding in a monastery, he serves not God but his own interests, while he rejoices that he is a prelate in order to obtain the pernicious liberties of the flesh, and fraudulently provides for his own future from the goods of the monastery. This disorder, moreover, is seen especially in those who, on any pretext, resign their office, to whom, as the reward of their stewardship, as if they had been bishops, an annual pension is assigned from the goods of the monastery. This is not the manner of those who seek the Lord; this is not the way of the monks of old. When you resign the pastoral office for God’s sake, resign it simply; do not demand anything besides food and clothing, if you do not wish to sin with those who have private property. You are a monk; you were a monk before you became abbot; you will remain a monk after the office. Why, then, should you demand a pension, since you know that you are a monk? Just as the fault of simony is committed by buying prelacies, so by demanding a pension for the resignation of an abbacy one sins against the Rule. What then? Do we condemn those who, resigning the office of pastoral care without fault, have received annual provisions from the goods of the monastery? Far be it. We do not forbid necessities, since we deny superfluities. Yet the man who is a true monk and a lover of God is content with the provision of the Rule even after an abbacy.

    How monks, citizens of the lowest region, are disordered toward one another. Article 4.

    Carnal [unclear] are disordered toward one another in many and various ways, because those who, stirred up by animal passions after the manner of beasts, do not direct themselves according to the right judgment of reason. It is no wonder if they overturn the order of fraternal conversation. For an unruly and disturbed conscience always presumes, and an evil mind never has the joys of peace, but is continually shaken by the sorrow of vices and is inwardly tormented by the everlasting fires of crimes. Thus monks, citizens of the dark region, blinded by evil and disordered affections, do not consider the end of the monastic profession; they love nothing but the advantage of the present life; they neglect their own salvation; they do not rise up to the love of eternity.

    First, therefore, they are very disordered toward one another when they cast aside the intellectual regard that ought to be had for their brothers; when they do not notice the image of God in man; when they do not think of the common share of grace and glory infused in human beings and to be granted in the future; nor do they take care to show one another the love of fraternal fellowship. They live with one another like horse and mule, concordant in bodily appearance, because whatever is pleasing to sensuality they love; whatever accords with reason they do not admit. One loves another not because he is a man, but because

    is similar to an affection of sensuality. For the carnal man loves in a man not virtues, not religion, not, finally, nature itself, but flesh or blood, but the quality of the body. Therefore, since the love of carnal persons is carnal, it is easily changeable on occasion. For the citizens of this lowest region venerate similar ways, and monks always embrace monks like themselves with affection. Him whom God has loved from eternity the disordered cenobite persecutes; him whom God spurns because of his demerits, this man venerates as a saint.

    Secondly, cloistered men are disordered toward one another by reason of dissimilarity, when either the seniors, stirred up by austerity and pride, despise their juniors, or the juniors obstinately set themselves against their seniors. And this disorder is proved to be very contrary to the holy Rule, which commands seniors to love juniors with paternal affection, and enjoins juniors humbly to obey their seniors for God's sake. But when the seniors, citizens of this lowest region, withdraw paternal affection from the juniors, the lesser men blaze up into grave hatred; and when the young consider themselves unjustly despised by them, they daily accuse their depraved ways. Therefore weak young men learn the wrong ways of their seniors, and, as the proverb says, just as they see the greater men sing, so too the lesser men dance.

    Thirdly, monks who cast away good zeal and mutual obedience, and take up the kind of zeal that is evil and forbidden by the Rule, are badly ordered toward one another. By words and deeds they commit various injuries against one another. One strives, out of eagerness to rival, to watch another for evil; one is provoked by another to inflict insult. They mutually hold their weaknesses ready against each other; they are always panting for vengeance. Zeal for regular discipline is despised; the passion of indignation and bitterness rules. They meet one another with faces turned away; by fitting signs they make manifest how much hatred lies hidden in the breast. Not so the impious, not so: for whoever pursues his brother with hatred is proved a murderer and unworthy of the kingdom of God. O wretched condition, always, of carnal monks, which is the nearer to hell the more alien it has been from the fear of God. For whoever, through evil zeal, delights to be discordant in the school of peace imitates not angels but demons. For indeed, just as a brute animal does not abandon the savagery of its nature, so a bestial monk does not withdraw from the worst zeal.

    How monks, citizens of the lowest region, are disordered toward themselves

    Carnal monks, citizens of the lowest region, are disordered in nothing more than toward their own selves. For they cast away every consideration of themselves; to what end they were created they do not attend. Article V.

    [unclear]: because, while each one pollutes himself with the filth of vices, the wicked mind withdraws from the original rectitude of its condition. Nor is it any wonder if, toward others, he becomes outwardly a disordered cultivator of the lowest region, who, confused within himself by the various passions of the flesh, is inwardly scattered. For Scripture says: He who is evil to himself, to whom will he be good? The right order of the human condition established that the flesh is to be subjected to the spirit; the spirit is commanded to be subject to him from whom it received the form of being. But among carnal minds the order of reason is perverted, when the flesh rules over the spirit, and reason, which according to the force of understanding implanted in it ought to have governed all things, is suffocated by the pleasures of the flesh and does not hasten by command toward the rectitude of judgment.

    Carnal monks, therefore, are disordered toward themselves through the vice of curiosity, because by curiously inquiring into another’s life they pass judgment, and do not amend their own life, defiled by all vices. They do not know how to correct great crimes in themselves, yet they proudly reprove others when they offend in the smallest matters. They diligently consider the speck in a brother’s eye, and excuse the beam clinging in their own eyes as if it were nothing. They subject their affections to sensuality, and, the judgment of right reason being spurned, they live carnally like beasts; passion frequently stirs them to anger, and the fury of envy inflames them against their neighbor. With anxious mind they demand vengeance upon their brothers, which, often blinded by excessive fury, they bring back not without harm to themselves. But disordered citizens cannot long lie hidden in secret, for the more they remain unknown to themselves through elation of mind, the more through blind judgment they become manifest to others. For a proud and disordered man is said first to be ignorant of himself, because if he truly knew himself, he would in no way be proud. Since, then, disorder of oneself takes its origin from pride, we cannot describe this plague better than if we undertake to uncover its roots, descending by degrees toward hell. For just as the perfection of the spiritual life is comprised in the twelve degrees of humility, so the whole disorder of the monastery is contained in the twice-six degrees of pride.

    The first degree of pride, then, is called curiosity, by which monks badly ordered toward themselves neglect their own life and morals, and continually inquire into the deeds or words of others. At every time they accuse the negligence of the brothers; they reprove the life of the pastor; and the more curiously they desire to know outwardly the affairs of others, the farther they withdraw from themselves. But the vice of curiosity is most destructive to monks, because, when it has once invaded the mind, stripping it of all virtues, it makes it a dwelling-place of vices. It is a very true sign of infirmity to examine the deeds of others and, beyond the reason of one’s office, to occupy oneself with the faults of others. For the monk who, according to the definition of his name, is instructed to care for himself alone, scrutinizes the deeds of others not without manifest danger to his salvation. But whoever [unclear] himself by the vice of curiosity

    [unclear] subject themselves; they soon descend into the second degree of pride. For one always disposes toward another, and no sin rules alone over proud monks.

    The second degree of pride, therefore, is lightness of mind and the unstable occupation of a wandering heart. Into this degree of disordered conduct carnal monks fall through various affections, which they have contracted sensually from the vice of curiosity. But the true coenobite must remain steadfast in his holy purpose, because when lightness of mind is admitted, the constancy of virtues is scattered in the heart. It is a sign of a disordered mind to run through various images of things and always to generate new forms of sensual affections.

    The third degree of pride is called vain gladness, which is produced from the lightness of mind of a disordered man. Carnal monks fashion for themselves images of affections; when these present themselves as pleasing to sensuality, they rejoice, but when the opposite occurs, contracting heavy indignation, they slip into various temptations. But that is not true joy which takes its beginning from anywhere other than God; nor will gladness long endure which has not taken its course from the love of God. And therefore disordered men, through vain gladness, fall into open boasting, while [unclear], as we have said, arises from vain gladness, which is called foolish boasting. Into this carnal monks fall when, magnifying themselves before others, they exalt themselves. If they have done anything good, they boldly bring it forward in public, often falsely inventing even what they have not done. They desire to seem holy, learned, prudent, and noble, and they invent many things by cleverness of wit, so that they may appear glorious outwardly to men, while they are not unaware that inwardly they are empty of the merit of virtue. If you begin to praise anyone before them, at once they rise up in opposition; they say many vicious things against him, because, while they desire to show themselves alone praiseworthy, they do not allow anyone else to be praised before them.

    The fifth degree is singularity. Into this degree of pride cloistered men fall who have presumed through boasting that they excel others either in merit or in knowledge. Hence, lest they appear like the rest in their manner of life, out of pride alone they show themselves singular in all things. This singularity of the proud is reprehended in a monastery, where the rule commands all to live in common. The proud, as Saint Bernard bears witness, when they prefer themselves to others for their virtues and wisdom, fall into such rash arrogance that they flatter themselves more over one fast while the rest are eating than if they had fasted seven days with the others. Finally, one little prayer of their own singular kind seems more advantageous to them than the whole psalmody of one night. During the meal they carry their eyes around the tables, and if they see anyone eating less, they groan and begin to grieve that they have been defeated, cruelly withholding from themselves what they had provided for necessary sustenance. These proud cloistered men are strenuous in their singular practices; in

    the opposites of the lazy. They keep watch in bed; in choir and at the regular reading they doze.

    The sixth degree of pride takes its beginning from the fifth; it is called the arrogance of the proud. For indeed, when disorderly cloistered men, through a zeal for singularity, begin outwardly to appear different from others, they are inflamed into a greater madness of arrogance; and whatever is said by people in their praise, the fools judge to be true. O lamentable folly of the proud: since in all matters they believe no one else more than themselves, yet concerning themselves alone they believe themselves less than another. Whatever praise of themselves they hear from the unskilled, they ascribe not to the ignorance or goodwill of the praiser, but to their own merits. But whoever is pleasantly fed on human praises is held before the Lord to be empty of every virtue and full of arrogance.

    The seventh degree of pride is born from the preceding one; it is called the presumption of the proud. Into this fall all the arrogant, who believe themselves individually to be something great. Concerning them Bernard says: He who thinks that he surpasses others, how shall he not presume more of himself than of others? He sits first in the community; in counsels he answers first; uncalled, he approaches; not ordered, he thrusts himself in; he reorders what has been ordered; he rejects what has been done by others. Whatever he himself has not done or ordered, he thinks was not rightly done nor handsomely ordered. He judges those who judge; he prejudges those who are about to judge. For one to whom God does not suffice in the heart seeks consolation in external things in vain.

    The eighth degree of pride is called the defense of sins, because it is begotten from presumption. For a presumptuous monk always thinks himself better than all; if he has committed any sin, he either stubbornly denies it, or, if he has been convicted, excuses it in many ways. For how will he be able humbly to confess his fault, who does not acknowledge himself guilty? If you wish to chastise such a man for his offenses, you always make him worse. Therefore whoever, when corrected for any matter, has turned aside into words of malice, whoever opposes to argument excuses for sins, falls into this descent of death, opposed to the fifth degree of humility. Now the presumptuous man who is found to have fallen into this degree of pride tries to excuse his sin in various ways. For either he says, “I did not do it,” or “I did it indeed, but I did well,” or, if badly, “not very badly,” or, if very badly, “not with evil intention.” And if he has been convicted of malice, at once in his own excuse he takes up another’s counsel. But he who does not fear insolently to deny or defend even things that are fitting and manifest will never reveal hidden things according to the rule to his abbot. But when he comes to confession, he will cloak the truth with a feigned mind; so that he himself may be able to escape confusion, he strives to bring forward into the midst the negligences of others. Inwardly ill-ordered, beneath and presumptuous, in confession he cloaks his own faults; he confesses those of others. Always restless within himself, he examines the deeds of others; [unclear] all by one sentence

    [Unclear] he seeks to live; he thinks that there is no charity among the brethren. But if his vain presumption has been detected through the diligence of the confessor, he at once seeks another confessor. If the abbot begins to oppose him, even gently, the monk, lifted up, falls through disquiet of mind into a new degree of pride.

    The ninth degree of pride is described as murmuring or impatience, which very often dominates carnal monks. For the man whose confession is feigned, touched by one slight insult or penance, at once rises up into open pride; the deceit of simulated humility is disclosed. Nor can a feigned mind hide itself any longer, but it is compelled to bring out in public whatever lies hidden within. From then on, the proud cenobite, having lost control of himself, murmurs at everything; he obstinately accuses the judgment of his pastor, however just it may be; he gnashes his teeth. Moved, he grows angry; without reason, like a madman, he is thrown into confusion. But the proud monk given to murmuring, having despised the fourth degree of humility, falls into the tenth descent of pride, through which he runs toward hell.

    The tenth degree of pride follows murmuring, and is called rebellion. Proud and carnal monks fall into this, those who, still dwelling in the lowest region, devote themselves to murmurings. Hence Bernard: “Unless [unclear] looks upon the murmurer, so that at last, being converted, which is very difficult for such men, he silently acquiesces in the judgments of others, he soon, becoming brazen and shameless, will fall the more ruinously into this degree, the more desperately he fails to restrain the movements of his mind.” He always advances toward worse things; and he who before had arrogantly despised his brothers in secret now also openly shows, what is more serious, that he despises his master. But the chastisement of divine judgment does not allow this degree of pride to pass long unpunished, since monks rebellious against their pastors are frequently consumed quickly and by a miserable death. For some, withdrawing from the order, become apostates; others, because of grave crimes, foul prisons; some, expelled from monasteries, wander as vagrants and wretched men in exile. Many, struck horribly by the Lord, in despair [unclear] to the lower regions. For it is written: “He who resists authority contradicts the ordinance of God.” And again the Lord says concerning the prelates of the faithful: “He who despises you despises me.” What will you say to these things, rebellious monks? Will you cite laws to me, whose truth you corrupt? But I dare to say what I wish you were ashamed to hear. The presumption of law will not save you, rebellious monk, in the strict examination of God, you who now proudly despise the obedience of subjection. Law commands obedience; it requires humble subjection in the order.

    Rebellious monks next fall into the eleventh degree of pride, which is the freedom to sin, those who despise not only the corrections and exhortations of the brethren, but also those of the prelates. For indeed, while rebellion against the command

    takes [unclear] upon himself; boldness in sinning is born, because he who despises the authority of correction already commits all crimes as though lawfully. The love of God voluntarily restrains good cenobites from sins, and fear restrains the weak. But where neither the love of God nor fear of correction penetrates the monk, then the mind, through rebellion and the habit of sinning, draws near to hell. For Scripture says: When the impious man has come into the depth of evils, he shows contempt. What does he contemn? He contemns God, despises men, and does not know how to seek the salvation of his own soul.

    Therefore he falls into the twelfth degree of pride who, through boldness in sinning, runs into an evil habit. This is the nearest descent to hell; this is the path of hell; this is the swift road to the region covered with the darkness of death. Whoever has once fallen into this degree of the habit of sinning rises again only by the strong hand of the merciful God, because when he does not resist habit, the necessity of sinning is born. For wickedness always advances toward the worse, and as it is always falling it falls more deeply.

    Behold, these are the twelve degrees of pride, through which one descends to hell; whoever desires to escape them should always take care to guard himself in the observance of humility. In these twelve evils every unworthiness of vices darkens the cenobite, causes the disordered monk to turn toward himself, and in his morals changes a man into a most savage beast. The end of these things is destruction, and unless before the death of the flesh the remedy of penitence intervenes, the progression of evil degrees condemns the monk to burn without end. But whoever, disordered toward himself, has once fallen into the first degree of pride, unless he strives to rise through penitence from all of it, soon casts himself headlong into the second and consequently into all the rest in order. The sum of the disorder of carnal monks toward themselves is expressed in these degrees of exaltation, through which they show themselves to be disordered citizens of the lowest region. But what we have said about the disordered and proud monk, we must also understand concerning the prelates of the lowest region.

    In what manner the citizens of the lowest region [are disordered]. Article VI.

    Whoever, established in a monastery, neglects to order his inner affections to the purity of his holy purpose frequently also exceeds measure enormously in outward things. For monks disordered toward God are consequently deemed disordered toward all things. For just as a good cenobite, united to the divine will through love, considers all things according to the right rule of the order with a simple eye, so one turned away from God through disordered affections sins even in the good things which he uses badly. Therefore carnal monks, cultivators of the lowest region, are not only badly disordered toward the soul, but also toward the substance of the monastery

    [unclear]. For upon inward confusion in the mind there follows outward disturbance of the body, and the one is shown by the other.

    And first, indeed, with regard to the property of the monastery, the citizens of the lowest region are badly ordered when they demand that these things be granted to them in improper order, or by any means usurp more than the usage of regular institution permits. For our Rule commands that all necessary things be given to monks; it utterly forbids superfluous things.

    Second, those make bad use of the property of the monastery who do not fear to give and receive contrary to the master’s prohibition, or who, in things entrusted to them, faithlessly commit deceit and fraud. For a monk who, at his own pleasure, without reasonable cause, contrary to the Rule, in any way dissipates the property of the monastery without permission, sins against the Rule like an unfaithful proprietor and a falsifier.

    Third, monks or abbots show themselves disordered with regard to the property of the monastery when they indulge in unlawful uses and commit theft and sacrilege, since they turn the property of the monastery to illicit uses. For the substance of the monastery, dedicated to God, is commanded to be guarded like the vessels of the holy altar, lest it be dissipated in any way through negligence. But he who forbids the goods of cloistered persons to be spent uselessly would by no means grant that they be disbursed for sin into shameful uses. What account, then, will monks and rectors of the lowest region owe to our lawgiver in the strict examination, who do not fear to dissipate the property of the monastery upon parents, kinsmen, mimes, actors, and shameful men as an occasion and reward of sin?

    Fourth, carnal abbots and monks sin gravely with regard to the property of the monastery, who, to the detriment of divine charity and their own salvation, gather these things together too greedily. For, inflamed by the torches of avarice, they think of nothing but profits and money. Violating feast days, they do not observe them. They always desire to increase temporal goods. They do not notice the losses of charity. They grieve more for a dying beast than for a perishing sinner. Indeed, all these disordered cloistered persons are so blind that they consider avarice to be prudence and think riches to be reform. They join field to field; they call gain piety; and where they see temporal goods abounding, there they say that the best discipline is being observed. They refuse to expend even a few things for the common good of the order, because inwardly they have lost the order of true charity. They raise useless, ostentatious, and damnable structures on high. They buy precious vestments and ornaments less necessary for divine services. They clothe sacred things in gold and leave the poor of Christ naked. This avaricious ostentation does not befit monks, since we who are commanded to imitate the holy men of old are ordered to sell these things for the support of the poor. But a covetous monk and an avaricious abbot are as far from the purpose of holy religion as the devil is from heaven.

    Fifth, carnal monks sin with regard to the property of the monastery when they do not repay it with prayers. The alms of the faithful

    [They] cheerfully receive [unclear], but few render to the givers the suffrages of prayers. Of these, many citizens of the lowest region, when they have come to the order, serve not God but the belly: they desire that more food, drink, and clothing be given them than necessity requires, and those who in the world could scarcely have bread and vegetables for food, now, having become monks, refuse eggs and little fish.

    They importunately demand that large, varied, diverse, and delicate fish be given them; murmuring because of desire for flesh with the children of Israel in the desert, they cry out to their leader; they assert that they cannot eat eggs and peas. They always desire more delicate things.

    How the citizens of the lowest region are ill ordered toward contempt of the world.

    Article VII.

    The kingdom of God suffers violence, and the violent seize it. Therefore whoever desires to enter the heavenly kingdom by the weapons of holy obedience, whoever wishes to live to God under regular conduct, must do violence to the pleasures of the flesh and strongly despise the world with all its vanities. But carnal monks, citizens of the lowest region, who are ill ordered both toward God and toward the goads, are also ill ordered toward contempt of the world.

    And first, indeed, they are infected by the concupiscence of the flesh, because they are always burning with the fire of pleasure. In food and drink they are found excessive; in little beds and baths, delicate contrary to the rule. They prefer the desires of the flesh to the salvation of the soul; they do not seek the sweetness of inward conversion.
