    Therefore, wishing to recommend the elevation of the mind in the Lord Jesus to those celebrating before the approach to the altar, we have arranged the following prayer from that which is attributed to Saint Ambrose of Milan, which we believe to be sufficiently effective by the merit of the Lord’s passion. Accordingly, the devout cenobite who is about to approach the altar, if he has leisure and is freely able, may first say this or a similar prayer, or may prepare himself in whatever ways he wishes.

    Prayer Before the Approach to the Altar

    Highest priest and true pontiff, Jesus Christ, who offered yourself to God the Father as a pure, holy, and immaculate victim on the altar of the cross for us miserable sinners; and who gave us your flesh to eat and your blood to drink, and established that mystery in the power of the Holy Spirit, saying, “As often as you do these things, you shall do them in memory of me.”

    I beseech you through the pain of your wounds and through the shedding of your most precious blood, and the power of your most innocent death, and through your very body and blood, the great price of our salvation; I beseech you through this wondrous and inexpressible charity with which you so loved us, miserable and unworthy, that you washed us from our sins in your blood: have mercy on me and forgive me all my sins, and teach me, your unworthy servant, whom among your other gifts you have deigned to call to the priestly office, not by any merits of mine but by the sole graciousness of your mercy, to handle this mystery through your Holy Spirit with that reverence and honor, devotion and fear, with which it ought and is fitting to be handled. Make me, I beseech you, always to believe and understand, to feel and firmly hold concerning so great a mystery that

    to [unclear] and to think what pleases you and what is expedient for the salvation of my soul. May your good Spirit enter into my heart, sounding there without sound, and without the noise of words speaking within me the truth of such great mysteries. For they are exceedingly deep, and covered with a sacred veil. Because of your great mercy, sweetest Lord Jesus, grant me to celebrate the solemn rites of the Masses with a pure heart and a clean conscience. I pray you, by the sweetness of your most holy heart, most loving Savior, cleanse my heart from all vain, impure, harmful, and unlawful thoughts, so that it may become a worthy dwelling-place of your love, now and without end forever.

    I beg you, O lover of humankind, sweetest Lord Jesus, through all the power of your most holy passion, drive away from me the spirit of self-exaltation and pride, vainglory and envy, lust and blasphemy; and fill my soul with the virtue of charity and innocence. King of the virtues, Jesus Christ, lover of [sacred?] chastity and integrity, I beg you, by the most holy virginity of the most blessed mother of God and undefiled Virgin Mary, and by the purity of your most reverend body, extinguish in me, with the heavenly dew of blessing, the tinder of burning lust, so that the brightness of all purity may be and remain in me. Mortify in me, I beseech you, the goads of the flesh, and all lustful stirrings and disordered affections; and give me true and perpetual chastity, together with the other gifts of yours that truly please you, so that at all times, with an unstained body and a clean heart, I may be able to offer to you the sacrifice of your body and blood.

    I know, Lord, and truly know, and I confess this very thing to your goodness, that I am not worthy to approach so great a mystery, because of my very many sins and my many negligences. But I also know, and with my whole heart believe and with my mouth confess, that since you are almighty, you can make me worthy: you who alone justify the ungodly, and can make the clean from the unclean. Therefore I pray you by your omnipotence: grant to me, your unworthy servant, true contrition for my sins, and pure devotion, and most fervent compunction in your love, so that I may be able to offer to you this most holy sacrifice with fear and reverence, with purity of heart and a fountain of sweet tears, with spiritual gladness and heavenly joy, with humility and fervor of charity. O sweetest Lord Jesus, grant me your mercy in this hour, so that my mind may feel the sweetness of your most blessed presence, and the devotion of the holy angels around me, and its own peaceful elevation in you.

    Take away from me, Lord Jesus, all my iniquities, and graciously kindle in me the fire of your love. Do not be angry with me, O Jesus, ineffable good, nor withhold from me the abundance of your compassion. For it is not in my own justifications that I pour out prayers before your face, Lord, but in your many mercies. Take away from me, Lord Jesus, a stony and hard heart, and give me

    [unclear] a heart of flesh and contrition, that it may fear you, love you, cherish you above all things, delight in you alone, follow you, and enjoy you forever.

    O most merciful Lord Jesus, I beg you by the most holy mystery of your body and blood, by which in your holy church we are daily fed and given drink, washed and sanctified, and made sharers in your one supreme divinity: grant me your holy virtues, adorned with which I may be able to approach your altar with a good conscience, so that these heavenly sacraments may become salvation and life for me. For you said with your holy and most blessed mouth: The bread that I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world. If anyone eats of this bread, he shall live forever. O sweetest bread, heal the palate of my heart, that I may feel the sweetness of your love.

    Heal, Lord, my heart from every sickness, so that it may feel no sweetness besides you, seek no love besides you, love no consolation besides you. O most holy Jesus, bread of life and understanding, having in you every delight and every sweetness of fragrance, who always refresh us from yourself and in yourself never fail: let my heart eat you, I beseech you, and let my soul be filled with the sweetness of your savor. O holy bread, O living bread, beautiful bread, pure bread, who came down from heaven and give life to the world: come into my heart, and cleanse me from every defilement of mind and spirit. Enter into my soul; heal and sanctify me at every time. Be yourself my continual health and salvation of body and soul. Drive away from me the enemies plotting against me, so that, fortified by the sacrament of your body and blood, through you I may advance on the straight path under regular discipline, and after this life may come joyfully to your kingdom.

    Excuse for the lengthiness

    If this prayer shall have seemed too long to anyone, let him read whatever part he wishes, for we have divided the material set before him into short paragraphs, so that we might remove weariness. But he who wishes to read neither the whole nor a part complains in vain about lengthiness, since he is shown to be unwilling to pray either a long or a short prayer.

    Meditation before approaching the altar

    Finally, through meditation on the Lord's Passion, or at least on one of its more sacred articles, or several if the opportunity of time is present, let the mind be kept devout. I would call meditation on the Lord's Passion savory when a man, purified through true mortification, as soon as he has begun to turn over the Lord's Passion in thought, dissolves without violence into tears from mere [unclear], and from the excessive desire of fervor, as if into a certain transport of mind [unclear].

    prepares himself. In this way he will never be able to prepare himself better for celebrating than if, before approaching the altar, he always runs through at least one point of the Lord's Passion in meditation and with tears. For indeed, since the celebration of Mass was instituted by our Redeemer himself in memory of the Lord's Passion, a man never prepares himself for it better or more fruitfully than if he is more fervently set aflame through meditation on that most bitter Passion.

    The Elevation of the Priest's Mind to God During the Celebration

    With how great reverence, devotion, and purity of mind we ought to stand before almighty God at the altar, what speech could express, or what understanding could penetrate by grasping it? For there the true body and true blood of our Lord Jesus Christ are confected in an ineffable manner. There the Lord of majesty, truly present, is adored. There the invisible host of angels, attending upon its king, rejoices together. There the whole heavenly court adores Jesus, God and man. Therefore the greatest purity of mind, the greatest reverence and humility, are needed when we must stand before so great a majesty, lest the Lord Jesus, searching the reins and the heart, be able to find anything in us that offends him. Let all worldly anxieties withdraw far from here; let all thoughts depart. Let nothing be thought here except what pertains to the completion of so great a ministry. Let nothing move in the mind except what belongs to the office in the presence of Majesty: the miracle of divine majesty is being performed; the Son of God is sacrificed to the Father; the body of our Redeemer is truly received; the mystery of our restoration is celebrated. Therefore, standing at the altar, the priest should remember that he is attending upon invisible majesty, and should take care not to think of anything from elsewhere.

    After the Celebration, Diligent [unclear] of the Mind

    After the communion of the body and blood, the devout cenobite should give thanks to almighty God, and should guard himself throughout the whole day, by spiritual exercise, in the purity and devotion of mind he has conceived. He should direct his affections toward God with fiery rays, and not grow lukewarm in his holy purpose. Above all he should strive to love nothing in this world, but to raise his heart continually toward the fire of divine love, wholly stripped of all earthly affections. He should always consider how, from now on, he may order his life as if anew in the holy fervor of his way of life, and humbly dispose himself for the often repeated reception of so great a guest. Finally, during the day, amid the labors enjoined upon him, he should often offer some prayer to God the Father in the power and union of that sacrament, so that through the exercises of holy communion and regular obedience he may kindle himself more fully in divine love. And this divine love we attain especially through the power of this venerable sacrament, if

    may we be renewed through the grace of compunction, by communicating more often in the remembrance of the Lord’s passion. For truly the devout mind of a man, through communion of this most sacred sacrament, is kindled by its effective operation into the fervor of divine love; and, having utterly denied itself, it is transformed into Christ, united to him by grace. Therefore, the more each person, having denied himself through true resignation, offers himself to the Lord as a living victim in remembrance of the Lord’s passion, the more disposed he will be to celebrate worthily.

    Returning to the cell after private masses

    When the celebration of masses is finished and the thanksgivings have been completed according to custom, let the monk return to his cell; and, after first saying the customary prayer, as above at matins, let him recollect himself for a little while and grow more fully in the holy purpose of perseverance. Then, turning to the Lord, let him say:

    ¶ Prayer.

    I beseech you, most sweet Lord Jesus, by the power of your most holy body and blood, which I have received, though unworthy: grant me the sweetness of your love, sincerity of brotherly affection, strength in temptation, purity in heart, and discipline in conduct, so that, by your bounty, I may satisfy my profession and continually advance in your most holy love. Then, until the first signal for choir, let him read something good, meditate, or pray; or certainly let him write, and fervently apply himself to the work enjoined on him by obedience.

    At the first signal for choir before [unclear]

    When the first signal has sounded for the hour that is customarily put before high mass, the monk of the community, immediately putting aside everything he has in his hands, should read the preparatory prayers for choir, just as they were set out in order above before matins. Afterward let him go to choir with reverence and maturity, bowing and praying according to the rite set forth above.

    At high mass. Consideration 4.

    At the ringing for high mass you will be able to read the due hour concerning the Holy Cross, and afterward, as much as time allows, to recall to memory something from the prologue placed before the private masses. For the sum of our salvation is placed in the merit of the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ; nor is any good work believed meritorious for us unless it is offered in its power. Now the remembrance of this passion is performed in the celebration of masses, where the innocent Lamb, slain for us, is offered to God the Father in an ineffable mystery. Therefore from our only Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, whom we believe to have suffered for us, we truly hope for salvation. And therefore whatever the Church asks in the collects, she humbly begs God the Father that it be given to her through him. This, therefore,

    with regard to the merit of the Lord’s Passion, our devout monk should have it in his heart; upon this the whole office of the Mass should run back sweetly, as upon the lower millstone. For every Mass, of whatever kind it may be, which is said in the holy Church of God, is at all times referred to the merit of the Lord’s Passion.

    On the Introit of the Mass.

    We do not intend to expound the office of the Mass point by point, since each one of us can find many expositions by others; but we desire to give occasion for meditation to devout brothers, whom we know to be inflamed with inward desires. Therefore you can, in meditation, refer the first part of the Introit and the verse to the incarnation of the Lord, and refer the repetition with the Gloria to his nativity. Nevertheless, you must carefully consider what the Introit contains according to the literal sense, so that you may be able to find a spiritual understanding suited to you. For nothing is done in vain in the divine office; rather, all things are filled with mysteries and sacred actions.

    On Kyrie eleison.

    Kyrie eleison is Greek, and is composed of a noun and a verb; among them these are two words. For the first is kyrios, which means “lord”; kyrie is said in the vocative. The second is from eleeo, which means “I have mercy.” Eleeson, “have mercy,” is expressed in the imperative. Hence kyrie eleison is formed, that is, “Lord, have mercy,” by elision for kyrie eleison, since a vowel before a vowel can be elided for a better sound.

    Thus Kyrie eleison is said three times to the Father, that he who out of exceeding charity wished his Son to be incarnate of the Virgin and to die for us may also be willing, by his mercy, to help us in our necessities.

    To the Son likewise we say Christe eleison three times, in which we ask him himself to help us.

    We also utter Kyrie eleison three times to the Holy Spirit, in which we humbly invoke him himself, through his ineffable goodness, to come to our aid.

    On Gloria in excelsis.

    Then Gloria in excelsis Deo is said in the singular number, in which we confess the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit to be one sole true God in the Trinity of persons and unity of substance. Consequently, during that angelic hymn the monk ought to be very devout and, so to speak, singly attentive to each word, in which the gift of peace is promised to men of good will, and God is humbly adored by us in various utterances.

    At the Collects.

    When the collects or prayers are uttered by the priest to God, the monk standing on the steps should think of nothing else, but, listening to the words of the priest, should present his own desire to God in concord with them.

    At the Epistle.

    When the Epistle is read, you must attend carefully to everything, and give thanks to God with the greatest fervor of spirit, because, leaving aside the Jewish people, he mercifully willed to call you and your forebears from Gentile error to his faith.

    At the Gradual.

    During the Gradual, Alleluia, Sequence, or Tract, think how long a desire the holy fathers had, who before Christ’s incarnation longed for his coming. Afterwards consider with how many labors and injuries your Savior was wearied for you in this world for thirty-three years, he who voluntarily gave himself to death for your salvation. Then remember the long and dangerous exile of your soul in the flesh, so that through this meditation on present misery you may be able the more to inflame your affection toward divine love.

    During the Gospel.

    During the holy Gospel, with your mind raised to the Lord, give thanks exultantly, because the merciful Father willed you to be born of Christian parents, and because he made you a participant in his holy and most sweet teaching.

    During the Creed.

    When the symbol of the Catholic faith is sung, consider all the words and mysteries with humble fervor of spirit. Hasten at once to recollect yourself wholly within yourself, so that you may be able to give thanks for having been called to the faith without any merit of yours, and to raise yourself up to him through spiritual love. Think, if you can, or rather as much as you can, how great, exalted, and immense is the Son of God, who willed to be incarnate for you; how hard and bitter were the things he endured for you.

    At the Offertory.

    During the Offertory, apply your mind with the host to be consecrated in offering; weigh what is done there mystically. For the host is round and white. In its whiteness is set forth the purity, innocence, and suffering humanity of our Savior, to be offered to God the Father on our behalf against all our impurities; in its roundness his immeasurable divinity, set before us as a reward, is offered. Therefore say to the Lord:

    Prayer.

    Almighty God, I have no worthy gift to offer you; in the most sacred offering of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, your only-begotten Son, I offer myself to you as an eternal gift, and as a perpetual servant; and give me

    the continual fire of your holy love, so that I may continually be able to render to you pleasing service. Through the same.

    Prayer. I offer to you, almighty God, the life, Passion, and death of the same our Lord Jesus Christ for my sins; for the holy Roman and universal Church; for the supreme pontiff; for our bishop; for our abbot; for all my confreres; for the unity of our observance; also for our whole order; for the salvation of all the faithful; for the conversion of unbelievers; and for the redemption of the souls of the faithful who are in the pains of purgatory. Receive, I beseech you, holy Father, this my offering in union with that charity by which you received the same our Lord Jesus Christ dying for us on the cross, and may it be pleasing to you.

    During the Preface. [Strive?] to raise yourself from all earthly things to heavenly things, and to prepare yourself to praise the Lord with the holy angels. Remember that by the merit of the Lord's Passion you have been called to the fellowship of the angels, and take care to arrive at it through observance of the commandments.

    At the Sanctus. With your mind lifted upward, when the Sanctus is sung, glorify the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, God and Lord; humbly adore his majesty at all times with the holy angels.

    During the Canon. After the holy praise, during the Canon, you may take up meditation on the Lord's Passion, and offer it through each of the greater principal articles to God the Father for yourself, or for others, or for any need. Say, therefore, in this way:

    Holy Father, I offer to you the bloody sweat, or in similar fashion, and the tears of our Lord Jesus Christ, your most beloved Son, in that charity and union in which he voluntarily offered himself to you unto death for us: for my sins, or for that brother, or for this or that need. And I ask you, by the pain of the wounds of the same your most sweet Son, and by the shedding of his most holy blood, and by the virtue of his most innocent death: have mercy on me, or on that person; or grant us this or that, etc. Through the same our Lord.

    You may also act similarly concerning the other articles of the Lord's Passion, and enlarge them by offering them according to the intention of your devotion.

    If your mind has not been occupied in the higher things of our Lord Jesus Christ, you may pray to the Lord, who is truly present, in this way:

    You are the King of glory, O Christ. You are the everlasting Son of the Father. You, to deliver, etc., to the end. For it is read that Saint Thomas Aquinas prayed this part of the hymn to the Lord at the elevation.

    At the Agnus Dei. While the Agnus Dei is sung, [unclear] your mind to the Lord Jesus with singular confidence

    raise [it]; and pray suppliantly that he may receive you into everlasting peace. Direct your affection toward him for love of whom you have left all things; ask from him, through the reception of holy communion, steadfast progress in your holy resolve.

    At “Ite, missa est.”

    When at the end “Ite, missa est” is sung, see that your mind is lifted up with the holy angels returning into heaven, so that through longing you may deserve to behold the Lord Jesus presiding in majesty, whom, now sent to the Father in the sacrament, you can no longer see on earth. Therefore kindle your longing by the image of desolation, in the manner of those who are unwillingly separated from their friends. Say, then, in your heart:

    Meditation

    Behold, my Lord has returned to the heavens; he has left me desolate on earth. What am I doing here with mortals, I who have an immortal Lord? Why do I not follow him? Alas for me, because my sojourning has been prolonged; I have dwelt with the dwellers in darkness; my soul has long been a sojourner. I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ; but who will free me, unhappy man, from the body of this death? Most beloved Lord Jesus, O my hope, O God and savior of my soul, draw me after you; I shall run in the fragrance of your ointments.

    O my sweet love, do not forget me unto the end, but deign often to lift up my mind to you, so that, since while set in this mortality I cannot see you bodily, at least, lifted up in affection and desire in your most holy love, I may deserve more often to behold you in spirit in glory. O my salvation, O heart of my heart, most beloved Jesus, do not abandon me or despise me; be my gracious helper and direct me always in your most holy will, so that I may be able to please you [unclear].

    After high mass and the following hour

    After the end of the hour which immediately follows high mass, return to your cell with the customary reverence described above; pour out prayers to the Lord with fervor of spirit, as we taught after Matins; devote what remains of the time to meditations. Consider the foulness of sin: how it separates from God and condemns forever the one who is turned away and does not repent. Therefore take care to turn your will wholly to God with the firmest resolve, and to avoid the contagion of sin at all times with all your strength.

    On the regular refectory meal. Consideration V.

    When the signal for the meal is rung, feel heartfelt compassion for the sick, the needy, and the poor who suffer want, and, when you can do nothing else, pray to the Lord for them. Consider that among Christians there are many far better than you whom harsh poverty oppresses in this life; at this hour neither the food necessary for sustenance is offered to them, nor are even the thinnest garments supplied for bodily clothing. But you, a monk, although you are a despiser of the world, are clothed in the finest...

    with garments; you sit at table like a prince; food is set before you to satiety by brothers better than you; all necessities, even to the point of nausea, are ministered to you, an unworthy sinner, by the servants of God. Consider, therefore, what outcome this abundance of things will have in a monk, since you, who by entering religion professed poverty, now in religion feast more splendidly than the rich of the world. Take care, therefore, that you not be ungrateful for such great benefits of God. Live according to the rule which you professed; pray for those who contribute temporal substance to your monastery, that almighty God may mercifully grant them eternal life.

    On Reading at Table.

    When you are seated at table during the meal, be composed; do not look this way and that, but take care to eat the food set before you, only for the necessity of nature, with humility and thanksgiving. Consider carefully what is read at table, so that, just as the body is refreshed with its food, so the soul may by no means be defrauded of its own refreshment. Learn frequently, while eating, to lift your mind to heavenly things, and through the word of sacred reading, which is never lacking to us while we eat, sweetly to inflame yourself with divine compunction. For the true and inward worshiper of God, whenever he hears anything read, even amid feasting, about the bitterness of the Lord’s Passion, about the fervor of divine love, or about the kingdom of the heavenly homeland, at once groans from exceeding desire; his feeling is kindled in the ardor of love; compelled by exceeding sweetness, the man weeps. For indeed the mind that truly loves the Lord Jesus, as soon as it hears his name or looks upon the image of the Crucified, is dissolved in compunction and by affection is lifted to his feet or embraces.

    For Giving Thanks.

    When the meal has been completed, give thanks to the Lord; and while you go to the church under the psalm, direct your mind upward; intercede for benefactors living and dead. If after the thanksgiving you add some special prayer for the dead, you do well.

    On the Regular Reading.

    Returning from the refectory to your cell, if it is not a fast day, complete the customary prayer; then read something good for edification, meditate, or do the work that has been assigned to you, or write. But if it is a fast day, take up the volume of your study and enter the place of the regular reading; sitting with the others, read in silence whatever you wish. But when you have been asked by the presiding officer to say something good, say a few things and use-

    [unclear]; without curious citations you shall answer humbly. Do not use lengthy speech, nor bring forward the vain curiosities of secular persons into the midst, besetting your brothers, or entangle your superiors in your speeches; but express the conception of your mind simply in a few words, unless perhaps the presiding officer, for a definite reason, has ordered you to make a longer speech.

    The exercise of the monk after dinner until vespers. Consideration VI.

    After the reading, when you have returned to your cell, you ought always to put some prayer before your works, and in all the things that you do to ask for God's help. And when you are in your cell, do not be idle, but always do some good thing, especially what the obedience of the abbot has enjoined. Now pray, now write, read something good or meditate; for the cell makes an idle monk either a beast or a demon. But of these matters we shall speak more fully below in their proper place. Take care to spend your time usefully, since very soon you are going to render an account of all things to God.

    On dwelling in the cell and on the works to be done in it.

    There are three places in one of which the devout monk who loves God ought more frequently to be found: namely, in the church, in the cell, and, at its proper time, in the refectory. But wandering through the monastery is not permitted, because it is written of the evil, the reprobate, and the gyrovagues: “The wicked walk in a circuit.” But of the just man Jeremiah says: “It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke of the Lord from his youth; he shall sit alone and keep silence, because he has lifted himself above himself.” Now there are five principal works of the cell: the first is to attend to commands; the second is to read usefully; the third is to persist in suitable meditation; the fourth is to pray frequently; the fifth is to rest fittingly. Let us speak of these briefly in order.

    In the cell you must first attend to commands.

    First, then, when you are in the dwelling of the cell, learn to attend to commands, and not to prefer your idle devotions to obedience. For Scripture says: “Obedience is better than the sacrifices of fools, and to listen is better than to offer fat.” Therefore, if something has been enjoined on you to do in the cell, do not transgress the paths of obedience on any pretext whatever, but strive diligently to carry out the work imposed on you for love of our Lord Jesus Christ and for the merit of holy obedience. Hence Hugh, the lover of quiet, says: “Be gladly in the cell, and always do something in it that builds you up and is enjoined by a superior, reckoning that it is not within your right to leave it without permission, except for the necessity of nature.” You also have on this matter the prohibition of our most holy father Benedict in the Rule, who forbids you to go out and run about without permission.

    Secondly, in the cell you ought to read profitably.

    It is especially fitting for a monk staying in his cell always to read something good, and to occupy himself usefully in all things. For sacred reading overcomes the temptations of the devil, calms the fires of the flesh, makes one despise the world, and raises the mind to heavenly things. For Jerome, lover of divine Scripture, truly said: “Love the knowledge of the Scriptures, and you will not love the vices of the flesh.” Not all things are to be read by all monks, since one who is still weak in spirit must be imbued only with simple teachings. And Hugh says to the monk who loves simplicity: “Do not read in order that you may be considered more learned, nor read curiosities that do not edify, since vain reading begets vain thoughts and extinguishes the mind’s devotion.” Therefore simple things, not lofty ones, are to be read by simpler monks; devout things, not curious ones, so that those who, because of slowness of understanding, are not learned in higher matters may not become dissolute in vain things. But for those who are stronger in spirit, we do not forbid suitable studies, since all things are clean to the clean, and nothing that is read harms the truly devout. Nevertheless let no one claim for himself a strength of spirit that he does not have; rather it is placed in the abbot’s discretion who may seem fit for freedom in reading.

    Thirdly, in the cell you ought to devote yourself opportunely to meditations.

    Just as a flower arises from a root, so meditation is generated from reading. If the reading has been vain, the meditation too will be fruitless and useless. For meditation is the fruit of reading, and prayer the offspring of meditation. Therefore take care to devote yourself opportunely to holy meditations, so that you may also learn sometimes to raise the mind through the fervor of divine love into contemplation. Finally, meditation itself raises the mind and commits the study of reading to memory.

    Fourthly, in the cell you ought frequently to pray.

    The holy apostle admonishes us to devote ourselves to prayer without ceasing, because just as breath is always necessary for us for the life of the flesh, so continual prayer is altogether necessary for the health of the mind. For just as we are instructed toward good by readings, so by prayers we are freed from evil. For the Lord says in the holy Gospel: “Pray that you may not enter into temptation.” For prayer refreshes the hungry mind, extinguishes the fire of carnal concupiscence, instructs conduct, and drives away demons. If you wish always to be with God, pray. Let your prayer be pure, simple, and clean; let it be poured out to God through the fervor of love, and it will not be able to be fruitless.

    Fifthly, in the cell you ought to rest properly.

    He rests best who commits no evil. He rests well who despises all occupations of the world. Be quiet in the cell, so that you do not wander this way and that in any thought; be pure and tranquil in mind, so that

    [unclear]. For Saint Prosper says in his poem: "Wisdom fills a tranquil mind, free from cares, and will be the guest of a peaceful heart." And again he says: "Those who are at peace can search the law, provided that their hearts, free from the tumult of the world, are at leisure." Therefore, so that the mind, intent on holy studies, may be aided, let divine love overcome fleshly quarrels. Remain, then, quiet in your cell, and by loving you will be able to know the truth. For the mind cannot be tranquil and capable of divine wisdom when the body is restless. Hence Hugh says: "Be quiet in the dormitory, lest another be disturbed through you." But when you wake, or when you wish to sleep, let the memory of God's goodness always come before you with thanksgiving: how he himself always watches over us, so that he may guard us, humbly serving him, from every evil. When you go to your bed, you should first set before yourself something by thinking or meditating about God, so that amid holy thoughts you may sweetly be able to fall asleep. For as the occupations of one who is awake have been, so also will be the rest of one who sleeps, and such too will be his dreams. For the mind burning with divine love, whether sleeping or waking, will not be able to forget its beloved, just as the bride says in the Canticles: "I sleep, and my heart watches."

    At Vespers. Consideration VII.

    [unclear] After the signal, with the other things that are customarily put first, you can sympathize with those occupied in worldly business; and give thanks that almighty God wished you to be free from them for serving him. Then you can gather yourself back to inward things, or meditate somewhat on the Lord's Passion, until, when the second signal sounds, you go to choir. For in my judgment no meditation is better for beginners and those making progress toward compunction and devotion of mind than that which takes its beginning from the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ through unknown affections.

    At the Office for the Dead.

    [unclear] After the compulsion of vigils following vespers, you can say the hour of the Holy Cross, and afterward think somewhat about the immeasurable charity of God by which he loves faithful souls. Then, so far as you can, think in what great desolation those holy souls placed in purgatory are; how great the pain is for a spirit separated from the body and desiring to return to the center of its origin, not to be able to behold the face of its Creator by friendly enjoyment, but to be compelled to wait in pains and torments most grievous to it. For so great is the desolation, sorrow, and grief of a separated soul placed in pains and desiring to come to God, that no kind of torments known to us in this world could be compared with its sadness. There is no comparison, in our way, of bodily sadness [unclear] [unclear].

    [unclear] and of desolation, to the state of a separated spirit, and placed in the delay of its return to its own beginning. Therefore, as much as you can, have compassion on the desolation of the souls of the faithful groaning in the prison of purgatory, and pour out diligent prayers for them to the Lord. For although the almighty and merciful Father, by his justice, defers them from the kingdom, nevertheless he loves them with inestimable charity. Whatever good, therefore, you now do by praying for them, you offer as a pleasing sacrifice to almighty God. And when you come there, you will receive multiplied whatever you have done here for them in charity. For Scripture says: It is holy and wholesome to pray for the dead, that they may be released from sins.

    Passing Through a Cemetery or Cloister.

    But when passing through a cemetery, cloister, or another place of burial of the dead, do not forget your brothers and all the faithful departed; but, moved by charity, have compassion on them, and strive to aid them before the Lord in this or a similar way. Prayer.

    Hail, faithful souls; rest in holy peace. May he who redeemed you with his precious blood deign to free you from punishments and bring you to eternal joys, where you may rejoice and exult forever, blessed ones. Another.

    May God the Father, who created you, bless you. May Jesus Christ, who redeemed you with his most precious blood, bless you. May the Holy Spirit, who by his mercy and gift preserved you from eternal damnation, bless you. Amen.

    Read the Following Prayer Often.

    I beseech you, sweetest Lord Jesus, Son of the living God, through the pain of your wounds, and through the shedding of your most holy blood, and through the power of your most innocent death: have mercy on the souls of the faithful departed existing in the punishments of purgatory, and grant them the dwelling of eternal light with all your saints.

    After Vespers Until Compline. Consideration Eight.

    with prayers and customary inclinations, return, and there, on bended knees, give thanks to your most merciful preserver, because he not only mercifully snatched you away from the vanities of the world, but also guarded you in the order from many evils and dangers. Then consider how many bodily and spiritual goods the gracious [unclear], though you deserved nothing, has shown you

    [unclear]: and, what is greatest, he promised himself as a reward to you if you faithfully persevere in love of him. Be grateful and always watchful in prayer, so that you may burn sweetly in the love of God.

    At supper.

    When the signal has been given for going to supper, humbly prepare yourself to attend, and observe what we marked out above for dinner. After supper you may return to your cell and devote yourself to prayer or meditation until the signal is rung for the collation.

    At the collation.

    After supper, when you hear the signal for the spiritual collation, you should at once hasten to attend it with gravity, and hear the last reading of the day with fervor of spirit. For the word of holy exhortation that has been heard last will cling more firmly to the mind throughout the whole night. But if it is a fast, the collation is customarily observed in the refectory while drinking. Therefore be attentive to the sacred reading in every place, for where the word of holy exhortation is willingly received with attention, it cannot happen otherwise than that the mind is often lifted up.

    At Compline.

    When going to Compline, beseech the Lord that he may always make you despise all worldly and carnal things, and grant you to remain continually in his most holy love, so that, when the course of this present life has been completed, you may deserve to enter the temple of God not made by hand, and rejoice eternally in the Lord with all the saints. At the end of Compline, when you hear the signal of the Angelic Salutation being rung, you shall humbly greet the most blessed Mother of God and Virgin Mary, that by her merits she may guard you through the night and continually intercede with her Son for your salvation.

    After Compline.

    When Compline is finished, return at once to your cell, and, after the customary prayers have been said, take care to prepare yourself most diligently for the following recollection of the soul.

    On recollection after Compline. Consideration IX.

    Since we cannot persist altogether immovable in one state of mind, it is necessary for us to renew our holy purpose more often, so that as often as during the day, by wandering through the byways of sins, we withdraw from the one principle of our soul, the Most High God, so often by contrition and compunction we may return to him, with correction firmly purposed. Hence our holy fathers established for us that we should devote ourselves to recollection after Compline, and concerning our negligence

    to examine the negligences committed during the day, so that the purpose of holiness, which we know to be quite weak and infirm, we may renew to fervor of spirit through the continual exercise of recollection. Therefore our devout cenobite, wishing fruitfully and by useful continuance to recollect himself, ought chiefly to examine himself in five things in order.

    The first thing to be observed in recollection: examination.

    The rendering of account

    The first is the rendering of account, by which the cenobite is ordered to bring back before the eyes of his mind, for correction, whatever he remembers himself to have committed during the day by sinning negligently or badly or less well. Therefore, turned toward the Lord, with hands clasped, let him lie before his bed and speak in this or a similar manner.

    I give thanks to you, almighty and merciful God, for all your benefits, which you have deigned to show to me, an unworthy sinner and one deserving nothing at all, from my youth up to this hour; for although I have deserved no good thing, I have received many and innumerable gifts of your goodness. Would that I could worthily give thanks to you, the highest and unchangeable good; would that in your holy service I could praise you with a pure heart and clean conscience. But, alas, with weakness, concupiscence, and evil habit prevailing, I, who ought to have clung to your most holy love with pure heart and conscience, have offended you again and again by many negligences and faults; and as often as, according to the inward inspirations of your goodness, I have tried to rise to fervor of spirit, alas, I grieve that, raising myself up, I have fallen again.

    Behold, good Jesus, into how many faults, how many guilty states I have fallen today alone; how many vain, how many useless, how many destructive thoughts I have admitted in so few hours; how many useless and harmful words I have uttered; how many negligences and sins I have perpetrated in my actions this day.

    Woe to me, miserable man, who could not persevere even for one very short day in your most holy service without impurity of heart and negligence; who today have committed so many faults and various imperfections. I confess to your goodness, O most gentle God, all my sins into which I have fallen from my earliest age. At your feet, O most sweet Jesus, I place all the negligences that I have committed today; I ask pardon, which I am not worthy to receive; I seek grace, which I confess that I have so often received in vain. O most beloved mediator of God and men, Jesus Christ, do not despise the miserable sinner whom you willed to purchase with your own blood. I confess to you all the negligences into which I have in any way fallen today, and the faults that I have committed.

    Thus let the cenobite, prostrate in mind before the Lord, call the more serious negligences back to memory, and, humbly seeking pardon, bewail his imperfection. But especially let him consider if he has offended anyone by word or deed; if he has said anything against a brother; if he has committed anything against charity and reverence; or

    if he has knowingly grieved someone wrongfully. And generally, in whatever matter he knows that he has sinned against God, against himself, against his prelate, against his neighbor, or against the rule or the statutes of the fathers, let him strive to bring it back to the examination of this chapter; and concerning secret matters, in tomorrow’s confession; concerning public transgressions and breaches of the Rule, in the next chapter, let him faithfully and from the heart resolve to clear himself by accusing himself. Let him grieve for what he has committed; let him make satisfaction for what is [unclear]; let him beware of what is to be committed.

    Then let him consider the grave danger of offending God, whether the sin be venial or mortal. For Johannes Gerson, chancellor of Paris, says in the treatise On the Spiritual Life: Sin, even venial sin, is so much against God that, by his justice, he could damn a man eternally for it. But that he does not impute it to a man unto damnation proceeds not from justice but from his infinite goodness. And the holy bishop Anselm warns us that a man ought not knowingly to commit the least sin against God’s will for the sake of the whole world. For the most blessed pontiff Augustine says: No sin is so venial that it does not become mortal when it is pleasing. You might say: This opinion cannot be true, since if a sin has been venial it can never become mortal; but if it becomes mortal, it was not venial. But listen and understand. I concede that venial sin, considered in itself, cannot become mortal; but one and the same sin, which can stand together with charity, is imputed to another, in the same desert, from contempt and aversion from God. Blessed, therefore, is he who is always fearful; but he who is hard of mind shall fall into evil. He who neglects the smallest sins when he can amend them gradually falls into graver ones.

    Indeed, how greatly sin displeases almighty God is shown by the vengeance that follows. For so often do we read, in the sacred volumes and in the deeds of time past, of sinners against the Lord being gravely punished, that we may deservedly fear the pit of sin.

    How greatly even the briefest thought of a spirit turned away displeases him is declared to us by the fall of the first angel. For as soon as he showed himself disordered against the Lord by growing proud, he was cast into hell.

    How greatly idle and useless words are against the Lord, a sufficiently clear story in the Lives of the Holy Fathers warns us, concerning the infernal [unclear] appearing among brothers speaking useless things.

    How greatly evil and pernicious words offend almighty God was shown in the case of a five-year-old boy who was blaspheming, whom the devil, snatching him living from his father’s lap, carried off to hell, as is believed.

    How greatly deeds and negligences concerning one’s office displease him is shown in the sons of Eli, who neglected and cared too little for the rite of sacrifice.

    How greatly even good works done contrary to customary and promised obedience displease God, Saint [Astion?] taught us by his deed: although [unclear], nevertheless [unclear], he did not carry the customary waters without punishment. And we read similar things concerning many others.

    How greatly evil deeds offend God, since we can understand it from infinite histories, as I might say, there is no need to prove by a few examples.

    When, however, our monk, after having gone through his recollections, finds himself burdened by the aforesaid or by any other negligences or sins, however grave, let him take up the contrition possible to him for the past, a purpose of amendment and of firmly guarding against future things, and penitence for what has been committed. Let him therefore take the counsel of the above-mentioned chancellor, and, being compunct, say to the Lord:

    Truth I.

    Lord my God, I confess to your most holy goodness that in this way or that I have sinned against your will; for this I grieve vehemently, and because I have offended you, who are wholly good, I humbly do penance.

    Truth II.

    O Lord my God, who know all things, you know that, by your bounty, I have a good purpose, and I intend, with your help, to amend myself in the future according to my strength. Therefore sin is guarded against by prayers, by invoking God for help; by punishments, by inflicting penitence on the body; by flight, by avoiding the occasion of sin. Therefore, for the third truth, let him say:

    Truth III.

    Lord my God, I have a good will to make confession of my sins, according to your commandment and that of holy mother Church, according to place and time, from the heart, fully, without deceit.

    Whoever has uttered these three truths to the Lord from sincerity of heart, without falsehood in mouth or mind, however much he may previously have sinned, is now secure, if in such a state, even without confession in the absence of a priest, he should die; yet in such a way that he must make satisfaction in purgatory for what, by doing penance, he did not complete. But whoever, because of an obstructing will to sin, in which he is actually taking delight, or because of a wicked purpose by which he scorns to avoid the occasions of sins, cannot truly say these same truths from a pure mind, is in a state of damnation, and not even the pope can absolve him.

    Indication of Future Precaution.

    The second thing prescribed to be observed by a monk in his recollection is called the indication of the future. Let him consider what were the occasions for him of past transgression, and he will more easily guard himself from the danger of future transgression. For the pit of sin is never better blocked up than if the occasion of sin is avoided. And Saint Bernard says: Indeed, an indication must be made for the night that is coming on, by distributing one’s exercises according to the rule of the common institution. In these every debt is duly paid if the spirit is subjected to God and the flesh to the spirit; and if anything has been omitted through neglect or left imperfect, let it not remain uncompensated in manner, time, and place.

    Request for Suffrages.

    Third in the recollection of a good cenobite is the devout asking of suffrages, since he understands his own weakness very well and seeks help from those stronger. Therefore, as soon as he has completed his recollection, he turns to the holy and undivided Trinity to seek mercy; then he invokes the most blessed Mother of God; afterward he implores the prayers and assistance of all the saints. And here he is mindful not only of his own, but pours out prayers for the whole order and the Church.

    Blessing for Resting

    Fourth in the recollection is the cenobite's blessing for resting, by which he arms himself with prayers and entrusts himself to the divine goodness to be guarded through the night. Therefore, at the sound of the dormitory signal, or at the appointed time, as he goes to the place of rest, let him fortify himself with the sign of the holy cross and say with devotion:

    The peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, the merit and integrity of the blessed Virgin, the sign of the cross over each one, the power of the Lord's Passion, the blessing, guardianship, and merit of all the holy angels and of God's elect, be between me and all enemies, visible and invisible, here and forever. Amen.

    Prayer

    I commend myself this night and at all times into your wounds, most loving Lord Jesus, and I ask you, through the merit [unclear], have mercy on me and guard me from all the snares and illusions of the enemy, so that with pure mind and clean body I may be able to rise at the hours appointed for me and praise you with fervor of spirit.

    Discretion for Obtaining Rest

    The fifth and final thing to be commemorated in recollection is [unclear] for rest: just as penance should never be omitted [unclear], so also one should not wish to prolong it too indiscreetly to the destruction of one's own head. Therefore, when all things have been completed with discretion, let desire and fervor toward God raise the mind with tears, if it can; let it not confound the mind. But as you ascend your bed, carry something in memory concerning the Lord's Passion, or concerning the love of Jesus, or certainly concerning the glory of the heavenly kingdom, according as [unclear], and let something help you as you are carried into sleep, which may also receive you when you wake and restore you to the state of yesterday's [interruption?]. Thus the night will be illuminated for you like the day, and the night will be your illumination in its delights, so that you may fall asleep peacefully, rest in peace, and wake easily; and rising, you will be ready to return to that from which you had not wholly departed. Yet in all these things discretion must always be applied, lest either excessive meditation, hindering sleep, destroy the brain, or immoderate sleep, [unclear].

    ...let him entirely leave off meditation. For at this hour the monk should rather sleep than meditate, so that at the appointed time he may be ready to rise and well disposed for the divine office with cheerfulness of spirit. For an affection too much inflamed by meditation destroys the brain and the senses, and takes sleep from the eyes of the weak. Therefore let meditation in bed be brief, where great strength is not present in the head either by grace or by nature.

    On Manual Labor. Consideration X.

    Since our most holy father Benedict, in the Rule, commending monks who live from the labors of their own hands, declares them blessed, it seemed fitting to us that after the end of the day we should say something about this most holy exercise. For we read that this work is commended in many ways by the holy fathers, and we know that in it they made no small progress before God and men. For the holy Apostle says: He who does not work shall not eat. But what Augustine, more learned among the most learned, thought about this manual exercise, he shows most clearly in the book On the Work of Monks. We also read that those ancient and most holy fathers dwelling in solitude labored diligently in the work of their hands, so that they would not incur the danger of idleness, and, living from their own labors after the example of the most blessed teacher of the Gentiles, would burden no one. Would that we too, brothers, might deign to undertake this holy exercise of laboring with the same intention and goodwill as they did, so that after the end of our labor we may deserve to rest with them without end in the heavenly homeland.

    Four Things Are [to Be Observed?] by a Monk in Labor

    When called to labor, the monk should strive to show himself such in the things to be observed that he does not lose the merit of bodily labor through dissolution of mind. For we see many among monks go out to labor wrongly, whom we see seeking nothing other than comforts of the flesh. Among these, some, so that at the time of the regular fast they may have an occasion for eating, take up useless and less necessary labors. For they labor in order to eat; whether it benefits or harms the monastery they do not care. Others, so that they may run about here and there without the restraint of discipline, as though by occasion, have been accustomed to arrange various labors. Others, so that they may freely indulge in vain talk and frivolities, procure labors useless to the monastery. Others love external labors so that they may be able, as though by opportunity and without suspicion, to see and speak with people, I will not say secular persons, known to them and friends according to the flesh, not according to God. Others, because of instability of mind, unable to rest in the monastery, always [unclear]

    [Marginal note:] [unclear] things to be observed ... he strives, so that the merit of labor ... comforts of the flesh, see. Many among monks rightly [unclear]. Are both useful to monasteries? By someone’s speech, and also it seems toward God. But opportunely to come into the monastery, and also to see friends according to the flesh, also is. Nevertheless, whatever must be done in the monastery will now be had here.

    seem to pant after labors. The intention of all those who labor thus is not sincere, and therefore they do not attain the best reward of labor. But you, brother, when you are called to labor, take care to submit your intention to the regular institution, so that you love nothing other than the honor of God, the merit of obedience, and the usefulness of the monastery; intend nothing except the progress of the soul. And when you are engaged in labor, do not imprudently extinguish the fervor of the spirit; do not omit the exercise of spiritual conduct, but take care diligently to observe everywhere the four following things. In outward conduct be faithful, serviceable, and benevolent; inwardly, humble and devout; in speech, sparing and edifying; in manners, composed and mature. If you observe these four things in labor, you will always return to your cell a better man.

    Outwardly let the monk be faithful, benevolent, and serviceable.

    The first thing that must be diligently observed in the labor of a cenobite is that in laboring he should always show himself faithful to his monastery; that he should forestall the brothers, out of charity, in serving and ministering, or even in carrying heavier burdens; and that in all words and deeds he should show himself benevolent and tractable. And Saint Bernard, lover of God, says: A serious and prudent soul applies itself to labor, yet is not dissipated in it, but through it rather gathers itself into itself, since it always has before its eyes not so much what it does as what it intends in doing. For in every completion it intends the end; and the more truly it strives for it, the more inwardly, fervently, and faithfully it works with its hands, subjecting to itself the service of its whole body, in which the will creates use, and use, by exercise, supplies strength. The devout and faithful cenobite, who loves God in truth, does not spare himself in labor, but is accustomed to apply himself to the manual tasks imposed on him with such fervor, cheerfulness, and fidelity, as if he alone were compelled by his labor to feed all those established in the monastery. For the most prudent soul knows that it is spending itself wholly for God whenever it happens to labor for the bodily need of his servants. For just as spiritual things cannot long subsist in religious life without the cooperation of temporal things, so I do not doubt that one who ministers the bodily necessities to those serving God on account of God is to be called the servant of God. Therefore whatever a good cenobite can acquire for his monastery by his labors with right intention, let him know that he is presenting all that to the Lord. Yet let a monk always understand that he must labor in such a way that he by no means omits the monastic prayers, masses, and the other services of holy mother Church.

    But manual work undertaken out of curiosity and one’s own complacency is deprived of the merit of obedience before the eternal judge; and, as idle and presumed without the permission of a superior, is held liable to account. But the good cenobite desires to please [unclear] in every stealthy intrusion of idle

    of deed or thought: let him say to himself that saying of Bernard: If you were now about to die, would you do thus what you are now doing, thinking, or saying? But if, being now about to die, you would not do what you now do, you are most foolish, who, being about to die shortly, so boldly permit yourself works of death unto death. But if, since it is necessary, you desire to die well, do at no time what you would not do if death were already at hand. For whatever you now do, whether it is good or evil, you will find after death.

    Inwardly the monk becomes humble and

    Secondly, at the time of labor the monk ought inwardly to be devout, devout and humble; for if the fervor of inward progress leaves him, what he acquires outwardly through labor is of no help. Therefore, so that the soul may truly make progress in laboring, let it often recall to memory the degrees of good will written in the first region. Let it order its meditations on the Lord’s passion according to the fervor of devotion; in these, as far as possible, let it conform its own labors to the labors of Christ. Let him always be humble in heart through self-denial; let him be devout in affection through the fervor of holy compunction, so that the outward labor of the hands may contribute to the advancement and usefulness of the community, and the mind may not withdraw from the inward sweetness of divine love. If labor wearies the working cenobite, if heat burns, if untimely thirst presses him hard, let him call to mind how many labors the Lord Jesus endured for us, and he will bear all things more lightly. Drawing breath, therefore, let him say to the Lord:

    Most sweet and most beloved Lord Jesus. Prayer of one laboring.

    O King of heaven and earth, who for my redemption, born of the most pure Virgin Mary, lived among men for thirty-three years as God and man; who had great labors in walking, teaching, and preaching; who for my sake willingly and patiently endured thirst, hunger, heat, and cold: for all these things I give thanks to you. Receive, I beseech you, these very small labors of mine, however useless, which I humbly offer to your most holy majesty in memory and honor of all your labors and of your most holy passion; and may they be pleasing to you in that union in which your most holy labors were pleasing to God the Father. Amen.

    Let our cenobite, moreover, under labor, if time permits, turn over in his mind the principal articles of the Lord’s passion: first by commemorating them as though Christ were present in the passion; then by giving thanks on his knees; third, by asking mercy in them according to their likeness.

    Let him also recall to memory the ways of life of the holy fathers or the passions of the martyrs, and consider how great a reward and glory they now receive in their homeland for their labors.

    In speech the monk becomes sparing and edifying.

    The third thing prescribed as to be observed by a monk at work is that he should speak few words, and edifying ones. For Scripture says: “In much speaking sin will not be lacking.” Let a monk never speak without permission, if he truly desires to be good. But once he has permission to speak, let him speak only a few useful words, knowing that idle and scurrilous words are condemned by the Rule in every place. Let him establish for himself, by circumspection, such a manner of speaking in every place and time that by speaking he offends no one. Let him listen more gladly than he is pleased to speak, and let him not say everything that his mind suggests, if he fears the reproach of fools. For thus Hugh also says to the monk: “Do not pour out everything you know, like a vessel without a lid, which, as soon as it is tilted, pours out whatever it contains and lies open to every dust and uncleanness.” Carefully beware lest you ever seem, directly or indirectly, to seek your own glory, or to reveal to anyone, with a desire for boasting, or otherwise imprudently, whatever praiseworthy thing lies hidden in you. If you are silent about yourself and conceal yourself, you will be more pleasing; if you disclose and commend yourself, you will become contemptible before all and will be laughed at. Beware of idle words, because while we do not take notice of such things, we slip little by little into harmful things, from which arise either disturbances, or looseness of conduct, or grave gnawings of conscience. Be such in your inner way of life that, through love of spiritual meditation, silence always delights you more than talkativeness.

    In His Conduct the Cenobite Is Composed and Mature

    The fourth thing is that a monk, both at work and outside it, in every place, is commanded to compose his conduct and to show himself mature before men in all deeds and words. Let him be clean and humble in heart; let him be kindly and useful in speech; let him be modest and grave in his gait; let him be mature and exemplary in his whole manner of life. Moreover, the whole man is easily brought into conformity with the standard of discipline if the effort to make progress is kept firm in his mind at all times. For indeed, while a monk desires to make progress daily toward better things, he avoids every looseness and disorderly manner of life. For a firm effort to make progress has this as its property: it makes the soul that strives very circumspect in all things. But one who does not have a firm effort to make progress toward the better cannot truly be called composed, although he may seem mature to men. For feigned maturity is quickly dissolved into a fitting looseness of mind where the root of discipline, the fear of God, is not present. Therefore, so that our cenobite may always be composed within and without, let him strive to be truly rooted in the fear of the Lord. For he who fears God neglects nothing, and the love of God is not idle.

    What the Conduct of a Mo[unclear] Ought to Be

    of a monk toward other men.

    Consideration XI.

    Since, then, we have begun to speak of the maturity and composure that a monk must preserve before all people, it seems useful to us now to say briefly how he ought to present himself to each. For he is instructed to present himself in one way to his prelate, and is commanded to show himself in another way before his brothers and secular persons. For to his ruler, in the place of Christ, he ought to show reverence; to his fellow brother, charity; to those who wrong him, gentleness; to secular persons, modest piety. Therefore let the monk render to each what is his own, and he will be truly composed before God and men. What he owes to God, or to himself, has been sufficiently said above; now let us pursue what has been set before us.

    Let his conduct be reverential toward the prelate in the place of Christ.

    First, the conduct of a monk ought to be reverential toward the prelate, as the Lord says in the holy Gospel: “He who hears you hears me; and he who despises you despises me.” For the monk who withholds the obedience and reverence owed to his abbot does injury to almighty God. For, as our most holy father says in the Rule, the abbot is shown to hold the place of Christ in the monastery. Therefore whoever despises the vicar of some king undoubtedly contemns the king himself.

    But tell me, good brother, why do you withhold due reverence from your prelate, whom you hear to be the vicar of Christ? Perhaps you think him evil and wholly unworthy of such an office, and therefore suppose that it is permitted you to contemn him? Not so, brother, not so; rather consider whose place it is in which Christ’s vicar presides, and you will know that you must honor the one sending you, not the one sent. If you wish to be Christ’s disciple, consider always for what you came, and you will never deny reverence even to an unworthy prelate.

    For what did you come? Surely so that, according to the Gospel and the Rule, you might deny yourself for God’s sake; so that under another’s command you might serve as a soldier for Christ; so that with patience you might await the eternal reward for these things. Therefore, brother, do not, do not lose the crown of eternal happiness prepared for you in heaven because of displeasure at one man, which you ought not to exchange for the whole world. Remember that you have nothing except from God, to whom you owe all that you are and all that you know, so that you may fulfill his will and live according to his ordinance. But since you are not confident that you can understand the will of God, you ought humbly to obey your ruler, as his vicar to whom you have subjected yourself; nor ought you to examine either his life or his command, since it is permitted [unclear] to judge the shepherd. Indeed, in your profession you swore that you ought not to carry out your own will, but that you wished to obey the abbot in all things according to the Rule. Therefore the abbot is the lord of your will, not by his own assumption, but by or-

    by the ordination of God, whose vicar he also is. The handling of another’s property against the owner’s will is theft, and you know that thieves will have no share in the kingdom of Christ and of God. Therefore a monk, regularly professed to God and to his abbot, thereafter no longer has lordship over his own will; if afterwards he usurps that same will for himself, he commits theft and sacrilege. Nor will permission [obtained?] save the presumptuous man, if it was obtained by threats and insults. Your abbot, brother, is God’s vicar; to him you must render the obedience you promised, not as to a man but as to God, and show humble reverence in God’s place. For whatever is rendered by subjects to their ruler is without doubt referred to God, whose vicar he is. Therefore, since you have subjected yourself to your prelate for God alone and for no other cause, you should strive at all times to show yourself such toward him that he may freely command you to do or omit whatever seems expedient to him, and may in no way fear any insolences or disturbances of your mind. For if your abbot is compelled to fear you, his monk, the order of equity is violated; and where the disciple strives to be above the master, the Gospel is sinned against. Beware, therefore, lest you withhold reverence and honor from prelates. Beware lest by grieving them you offend the Lord; but take care to meet them, whatever sort they may be, with reverence, and to obey their commands in all things according to the Gospel and the rule. Believe me, brother, that the fault which is committed by a subject against a prelate is punished most severely either in the present life or in the future one. It is written: Do not touch my anointed ones. Whatever your prelate has commanded you, you ought to receive with such confidence that you believe God has inspired it in him.

    Let the monk’s manner of life be in charity toward the brothers.

    Second, the monk’s manner of life toward his brethren commands him to have charity, through which alone peace and concord are maintained in the monastery. Let our faithful cenobite always think upon and turn over in his heart the common joy of souls in eternal happiness, and let him continually direct the eye of his mind to the equal condition of souls, so that his thought may not withdraw from love of their future fellowship. If a brother has offended you in any way by word or deed, if he has been troublesome or hostile to you in anything, do not take up from this a disordered movement of sensuality; do not consider his present infirmity, but raise the eyes of your mind to the nobility of his soul, and weigh what fellowship in eternal happiness it is to have with you. For this purpose you ought often to bring back to memory the chapter of the rule on the good zeal of monks, so that more readily toward brotherly charity

    that you may be able to rouse yourself. Before all things, take care that you admit no displeasure against your brother; for he who is frequently angry with his neighbor is plainly proved not to love God. For whoever loves God with all his heart does not admit displeasure against his faithful brother. A monk ought to be established in such great elevation of mind that, whatever his brother has committed against him, by weighing the nature of his soul he cannot be moved.

    Let the monk’s conduct toward those who do injury [be meek]

    Third, the monk’s conduct toward those who do injury ought to be meek; and he then at last acts well if regard for the common future blessedness and companionship is always kept before him. To attain this meekness of spirit, our cenobite should learn to recall to mind more often the ways of life of the holy fathers, and faithfully consider with how great joy they received injuries. First of all, as far as possible, let him strive to imitate our Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who not only endured the injuries and insults of the impious with a most meek heart, but also prayed to the Father for his persecutors, that they should not perish. Imitating this example of the Savior, the holy fathers were accustomed to receive injuries patiently and meekly for the love of God, and, what is more, to love the very men who injured them. To these things let the cenobite recall to mind the degrees of meekness, which are contained, briefly enclosed, in these verses: Fit yourself. Strengthen yourself. Being gentle, bear contrary things. Preserve. Restrain. Rest inwardly with yourself. Correct prudently. Be merciful. Give wisely. By placing yourself below, by taking up martyrdom. For humility, if it has possessed the mind of the cenobite, makes him love injuries. The degrees of humility are contained in these verses.

    The twelve degrees of humility.

    The first of the righteous degrees fears the Almighty. The second puts reins upon the enticements of the flesh. The third subjects himself reverently to the abbot. The fourth, despising insults, patiently obeys. The fifth reveals the inner chambers of his heart to the abbot. The sixth holds himself vile and unworthy by his own judgment. The seventh believes himself to be lower than all. The eighth does nothing that the rule of the cell does not allow. The eleventh speaks the few words of reason. The twelfth always looks at the ground with bent head.

    On the same things, otherwise.

    Third, the monk’s conduct toward those who do injury ought to be meek; and he then at last acts well if regard for the common future blessedness and companionship is always kept before him. To attain this meekness of spirit, our cenobite should learn to recall to mind more often the ways of life of the holy fathers, and faithfully consider with how great joy they received injuries. First of all, as far as possible, let him strive to imitate our Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who not only endured the injuries and insults of the impious with a most meek heart, but also prayed to the Father for his persecutors, that they should not perish. Imitating this example of the Savior, the holy fathers were accustomed to receive injuries patiently and meekly for the love of God, and, what is more, to love the very men who injured them. To these things let the cenobite recall to mind the degrees of meekness, which are contained, briefly enclosed, in these verses: Fit yourself. Strengthen yourself. Being gentle, bear contrary things. Preserve. Restrain. Rest inwardly with yourself. Correct prudently. Be merciful. Give wisely. By placing yourself below: martyrdom

    See God; do not do your own will; let another rule you. Bear hard things; hide nothing in your heart; but seek even the lowest things. Be a peripsema; do not wander alone; restrain your tongue. Let laughter be sparing, speech grave, gestures humble.

    Note: Peripsema must be read and written so, not peripsime, as the ignorant read in the Epistle to the Romans; and it is called the filings and cleansing of all things.

    Let the monk’s conduct toward secular persons be modest.

    The fourth conduct of the monk toward secular persons must be modest.

    It must be modest, so that neither his familiarity with them is excessive, nor his separation indiscreet. Hence Hugh says: With regard to people, so far as it lies in you, beware of everything that can be for them a bad example, as it befits a faithful servant of God to advance in all things the honor of his Lord and to avoid his dishonor. Do not be familiar with any woman, even a holy one. For if they are discreet, you will please them more by this; but if they are troublesome, they are all the more to be avoided. Do not be suspicious. Be attentive to the sick in humble services. Be very truthful in words. Let your words be as an oath, and you will edify others. Love poverty. Be chaste in all things, and everywhere God-fearing.

    But in establishing all virtues and good morals, set before yourself that most brilliant and most perfect example of all brightness, the life and conduct of our Lord Jesus Christ, who was sent from heaven for this purpose, that he might go before us in the way of virtues and instruct us by his example, as by himself. Therefore the more the monk has taken care to conform himself to him in the way of virtues by imitation, the more, without doubt, he will be like and near to him in the glory of eternal happiness. Whatever you do, always look to him, and consider how he conducted himself in all things according to the Gospel and according to your judgment. For since he is best, he conducted himself best in all things. Say therefore to yourself: If my Lord Jesus were present, what do you think he would do about this, or what would he now say? Certainly he would act and speak in the best way; him I must imitate in all things to the best of my strength.

    General conclusion of all spiritual exercises.

    Consideration twelve.

    Wishing at last to say something, we say that the completion of all spiritual exercises consists in two things. First, in the knowledge and feeling of one’s own imperfection, so that the monk may always be conscious of his weakness and remain rooted in humility. Second, in the desire and effort to come to a higher conduct, so that he may always desire to advance in spirit toward better things, and may by no means withdraw from this effort. Every cenobite must at every moment direct his mind toward this effort of advancing; if he ever leaves it off, he incurs transgression of his vow and a very grave danger to his soul. But let the monk take care that consideration of his own weakness does not cast aside the effort of advancing; let him take care that the effort itself does not despise consideration of imperfection; but let these two so cling mutually to one another that they never withdraw from one another. But if excessive consideration of his own imperfection should try to cast down the mind, let him recall to memory what the holy Abbot Bernard said: “Let us breathe again, brothers,” he says, “because even if we are nothing in our own hearts, perhaps something concerning us may lie hidden in the heart of God.” These two considerations, of our weakness and of divine estimation, stir up great devotion in us, as the psalmist said: “I am poor and sorrowful”: behold the first; “your salvation, O God, has taken me up”: behold the second.

    Finally, it is necessary for one who wishes to occupy himself profitably in these spiritual exercises to have a joyful and free heart, and one removed from every anxiety or care of the world. For the Holy Spirit is a spirit of freedom and joy; he loves a heart free and joyful in God, and, so to speak, applauds one like himself. But just as a bird bound on the earth cannot lift itself up to heaven by flying, so a mind occupied with perishable things cannot raise itself to heavenly things. Nor is it fitting to cast down the spirit by too much frequency; otherwise the brain too is confused, and through dry custom one labors in vain. Therefore let the cenobite fervent in spirit learn always to persist in these things with moderation, and continually to refer by intention the cause of every exercise to God, who is the beginning and end of all goodness. Let him faithfully direct his effort toward fear and love of him, and fix his mind in deep humility, because he is not easily abandoned by God who is rooted in love.

    Here is the end of the spiritual exercises concerning the threefold region of cloistered persons.
