    Here begins the Compendium of Spiritual Exercise. Johannes Trithemius.

    Although the form of spiritual exercise published by us for the edification of cloistered persons could seem very brief to any devout persons who have leisure, we fear nevertheless that to those occupied in household affairs it may seem rather lengthy; while their thought is stretched out in continual solicitude in arranging the necessities of their subjects, the mind is easily wearied even in the briefest spiritual exercises. Therefore, lest our monks who are either given over to external matters, or less devout in spiritual conduct, should be able, on the pretext of lengthiness, to take refuge in their usual argument of excuse, we have been ordered to abridge the same instruction, so that the fervent may keep the greater one in their devotion, and the lukewarm may not omit the lesser.

    There follows the practice of spiritual exercise.

    Before all and each of the hours, in general, the devout cenobite should strive to direct his effort to this end: that he may desire with all his strength to magnify God in his heart through the root of his benefits. Let there be in him so fervent an ardor of devotion, so great a compunction, and finally so great an outpouring of tears, that whoever sees him singing psalms may be moved by his example to magnify the Lord. Secondly, let him remember to stir himself, so far as he can, to charity toward his neighbor, because love is directed toward God in vain if one’s neighbor is hated. Therefore, after all spirits of displeasure have been driven out, turned toward the Lord, let the most devout cenobite pray:

    Almighty, everlasting God, who, instructing us for the exercise of your [unclear] by the manifold creation of things, have commanded us to love you above all things with all our strength, and our neighbor as ourselves for your sake: graciously grant me the grace of your most secret love and of love for my neighbor, so that, after all movements of displeasure, aversion, and anger have been repressed, I may always love you above all things with a pure heart, and in no way withdraw from sincere love of my neighbor; so that, just as one member, joined to another member, suffers with the wounded member, so may my mind, sincerely loving my neighbor, deserve to be a member of our true head, Jesus Christ. Who lives and reigns with you.

    Another prayer.

    I beseech you, holy Father, almighty, eternal God, through the power of the most holy Passion of your only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ: enlighten the eyes of my heart, so that, pierced in spirit, I may see how often I have offended against your commandments; and, cleansed by your mercy from every filth of sin, may I never offend you hereafter.

    After Matins.

    When Matins have been completed, while you are still remaining in the church, or even when placed in your cell, take up for yourself the disposition of true resignation, praying thus:

    Prayer. Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, who at the morning hour, placed in the greatest anguish of your most holy heart, after threefold prayer most fully resigned yourself to the will of your Father: grant me, by the power of that charity of yours, perfectly to despise my own will for love of you in all things, and truly at all times to resign myself to the ordering of your will and of those whom you have set over me. Who lives and reigns.

    After Prime.

    After Prime, when, leaving choir, you enter the chapter-room, in memory of your most innocent Savior accused before Pilate, you shall form your disposition toward humble confession, praying thus to the Lord:

    Prayer. Most loving and sweetest Lord Jesus, who at the [unclear] hour truly confessed yourself the Son of God: have mercy on me, and grant me, through your innocence, the virtue of true confession, so that I may humbly bear any words of those who accuse me, and by no reproaches withdraw from the inward tranquility of mind. Who lives and reigns with God the Father.

    After Terce.

    After Terce you will recall to mind how many reproaches, how many mockeries and derisions the most innocent Lord Jesus endured for your redemption; in memory of him take up for yourself the desire of the sixth degree of humility, praying thus:

    Prayer. O sweetest Lord Jesus, who for us at the third hour were miserably scourged, mocked, derided, crowned with thorns, and spat upon. Grant me, by the power of all your sufferings, through the shedding of your most holy blood, always to be content for love of you with usefulness and the utmost [unclear], so that, in view of my sins, I may regard myself as an unworthy worker of humility, and nevertheless in no way grow lukewarm in your holy service.

    After Sext.

    After Sext, consider the Lord Jesus carrying his cross before all and then hanging miserably upon it, together with the other articles of his punishments; and, inflamed with desire for the seventh degree of humility, pray to him with fervor of spirit.

    Prayer. Sweetest Lord Jesus, who for our sake, miserable sinners, after the countless pains of your Passion, carried your cross to the place of your death while your most sorrowful mother looked on; upon which, cruelly fastened, given gall and vinegar to drink, and mocked in many ways, you were: I ask you, through the pain of your wounds, grant me pardon mindful of all my sins, the grace of holy compunction, a fountain of tears, the virtue of deep humility, and continual remembrance of your most bitter Passion, so that all that I am and can do may always serve you, and my mind may burn continually in your love.

    After None.

    After None be mindful of sweetest Jesus dying on the cross; and, falling in spirit at his knees, giving thanks with tears with as much devotion as you can, you shall pray thus:

    Prayer. I adore you now, O sweetest Lord Jesus Christ, King of heaven and earth, dying for me, a wretch, on the cross; and I humbly give you thanks for your holy Passion and most innocent death. O what shall I render to you, most loving Savior, for all that you have rendered to me? Behold, I offer myself to you; I desire to dwell continually in your most holy wounds. I ask you, through the power of your most innocent death: have mercy on me as you know how; pierce my flesh with your fear, and restrain in me all disordered movements, so that, inflamed with the fervor of your most holy love, I may love you with a pure heart, confess you as praiseworthy with my mouth, and in deed follow you, according to my strength, in humble conduct. I beseech you, most merciful Lord Jesus, through that anguish of your most holy heart which you endured on the cross when your most holy soul went out from your body: have mercy on my soul at its departure.

    The first hour after the meal.

    At the first hour after the meal, unless you have been occupied with higher exercises, in order to obtain knowledge of your own frailty, you shall pray to the Lord in this or a similar manner:

    Prayer. Lord God, who out of your great compassion created [me?] in the first parent from the clay of the earth, so that me- R

    mindful of my lowly condition, I would glorify you, my creator, in true humility: grant me, I beseech you, truly to know my frailty at all times, so that, while I consider that by my own merit I am vile and almost nothing, I may deserve to please you by your gift. Through Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with you.

    The Second Hour.

    At the second hour after midday, let our devout cenobite briefly recall to mind the gravity of his sins, by which, especially while living in holy religion, he has sinned against the rule; and, turning to the Lord, let him pray thus.

    Prayer.

    Almighty, everlasting God, who by the incarnation and death of your only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, have deigned, out of your mercy alone, to bring us wretched persons, dead in sins, to life: grant me, through the power of his most innocent passion, pardon for all my sins, so that henceforth I may deserve to serve you with a pure conscience. Through the same our Lord.

    The Third Hour.

    At the third hour after the meal, let our faithful cenobite remember his vows which he promised to the Lord, and especially the renunciation of all property, namely in possessions, judgments, and will; and, moved to compunction, let him pray thus to the Lord in fervor of spirit.

    Prayer.

    Almighty and merciful God, who with gracious favor sanctify and receive the vows of your servants offered to you from faithful devotion: grant me to render all things promised to you, through the virtue of humility, chastity, obedience, and poverty, with such purity of mind that I may deserve, by your mercy, to reach your kingdom promised to the poor in spirit. Through our Lord.

    After Vespers.

    After Vespers let our good cenobite consider that all visible things are vain; and, his mind lifted up to love of invisible goods, let him cry out to the Lord then with as much devotion as he can.

    Prayer.

    [unclear]

    Almighty, everlasting God, who wished to lead us through the visible things which you created to the knowledge and love of the invisible: grant me so to know the vanity of present things that I may always deserve with a pure mind to contemplate the eternity of things to come.

    Another.

    O God, protector of those who hope in you, without whom nothing is strong, nothing holy: multiply your mercy upon us, so that with you as ruler, you as guide, we may pass through temporal goods in such a way that we do not lose the eternal.

    Another Prayer.

    O God, who have prepared invisible goods for those who love you: pour into our hearts the affection of your love, so that, loving you in all things and above all things, we may obtain your promises, which surpass every desire. Through our Lord.

    After Supper and Collation.

    After supper or collation let the faithful cenobite clothe himself with desire for good zeal, and especially for souls, with whatever fervor of charity he can, and, praying to the Lord, let him say:

    O Lord God, greatest lover of faithful souls, who for the salvation of men wished your Son to die on the gibbet of the cross: grant me, through the example of the same your Son, always to make progress in good zeal, and to fear no labors, no adversities, for the salvation of souls, so that, strengthened by the fire of your love, I may dare to resist opportunely those who contradict you, and manfully set myself as a wall for your house. Through the same our Lord.

    Prayer.

    After Compline, his powers gathered together, let the devout cenobite enter alone into the secret place of his heart, and leave outside all cares and anxieties of the world, so that, free and released from all things, he may deserve to converse with the Lord Jesus through desire of compunction, and to be sweetly united to him through the fire of love. Therefore, having in summary recalled to the examination of memory the faults of the day, let him pray thus to the Lord.

    Prayer.

    O most merciful Lord Jesus Christ, who for our redemption wished to undergo a most shameful death: grant me, I beseech you, through the pain of your wounds and through your most holy blood

    the outpouring and the power of your most innocent death, the forgiveness of all my sins: that, with conscience cleansed, I may henceforth through the desire of love continually cling to you, advance daily in holy religion, and humbly submit myself in all things to your most holy will.

    To the Son.

    My body and my soul I commend to you, Lord Jesus Christ, this night and at all times, in the power and union of that love by which, hanging on the cross, you commended your beloved mother, the Virgin Mary, to the disciple. In that love, I beseech you, guard me from all snares of the ancient serpent, suppress the illicit motions of the flesh, drive far away foul and evil dreams, and repel the phantasms of the nights, so that in your peace I may sleep securely and, at the hours appointed for me, rise gladly to your praises. Amen.

    To the Father.

    Lord, holy Father, almighty eternal God, who graciously received us into your grace in the passion of your only-begotten Son: receive mercifully, I beseech you, all the good works that, by your gift, I have done on this day, in words, deeds, or thoughts, in the power and union of that charity and love by which you received the same your Son hanging and dying on the cross for us. To you, holy Father, in the faith and union of that charity, I commend myself this night and at all times, by which your Son, our Lord, now about to die, commended his spirit to you on the cross.

    To Saint Mary.

    Holy and immaculate Mother of God, Virgin Mary, I beg you, by the bitter passion and death of your sweetest Son: do not despise me, a wretched sinner, because of my unclean conscience, but remember that you are the mother of mercy, and pray for me to the God whom you bore, that he may mercifully forgive me my sins, make me his fervent lover, guard me this night from all snares and evils, and after the death of the flesh lead my soul to eternal life. To your protection, most blessed Virgin Mary, I commit myself this night and at all times, in the power and union of that committal by which your beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, now about to die on the cross, commended you to John his disciple.

    On the Memory of the Lord’s Passion.

    Since the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ is the gate of our salvation, through which the kingdom of heaven is opened to us, we ought, with whatever devotion we can, to exercise ourselves in it more frequently, because we shall easily obtain the effect of our prayers if, through the love of compassion, in the power of his wounds, we adore the Lord. Therefore, faithful cenobite, with what diligence I can I warn, exhort, and ask you that, mindful of the benefits of God, you wholly neglect no day on which you do not give thanks to your Savior for the bitterness of his passion and death. And if, for any reason, you are unable to pray at greater length, at least do not refuse to show yourself grateful to your Redeemer with one word. Thus the Lord Jesus himself revealed to his lovers, to whom he wished, that nothing is more pleasing to him, and nothing more useful to us, than to recall with thanksgiving the memory of his passion and death, and to admonish others to do the same. Receive, therefore, an abbreviated word, lest a longer prayer make you weary.

    With knees bent to the ground and hands joined together, say:

    I give thanks to you, sweetest Lord Jesus, for all the wounds, pains, and injuries of your most innocent passion and death. I beg you, by that same death of yours, have mercy on me now and in the hour of my death. Or thus:

    For your most bitter passion and most innocent death, Lord Jesus Christ, I give thanks with a compassionate soul. I beg you, have mercy on me. Or thus:

    I praise, bless, and adore you, Lord Jesus Christ, King of heaven and earth, and I give thanks to you for your holy passion, by which you delivered wretched me from perpetual death. I beg you, by the power of that same passion of yours: make me eternally a participant in your most innocent death.

    Conclusion of this Compendium by Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim.

    So that I may not be more prolix than is fitting, I here set an end to the Compendium. For that venerable company of abbots of our annual Chapter instructed me to avoid prolixity in this place, lest lukewarm and worldly cloisterers make weariness their excuse. If the Lord Jesus gives me a life free from cares, which I have always desired, I shall try to satisfy both my own intention and another’s request. For, at the request of certain virgins dedicated to Christ, I have resolved to hand down a rule by which every devout cenobite may exercise himself, in the Lord’s passion, against all temptations. If, in this, they remain for a few months exercising themselves as they ought, he will by degrees sweetly fly from the humanity of Christ to his divinity through the ray of love. For to those who desire to come to the love of God, continual meditation on the Lord’s passion opens an easy entrance, because, while the mind through compassion is pierced by the memory of the benefits of so great a lover, burning with tears and desire it is lifted up to love. You, therefore, cloisterers dedicated to God, who have no leisure to attend to many things, receive these few things: in them, although there may not be a continual fire of love, yet for those who persevere it will be able to be renewed.

    Praise to God and to his mother for ever and ever. Amen.

    Here ends this Compendium, in which the business of the whole spiritual exercise is contained briefly and selectively. By Johannes Trithemius, Abbot. In the year from the reconciled divinity 1516. From the workshop of Melchior Lotter.

    What was wrong: The old translation smoothed garbled OCR into confident but unsupported prose: it invented an imperative "wound me" from the broken word "ani|me vulnerate" (the tail of "make a plaster for your wounded soul" from the previous chunk), rendered "modo dum loqueris" (even now, while you speak) as "at death," turned "dum prodest … dum cauen[di oportunitas adest]" into the invented adverbs "prudently … cautiously," and dropped the clause "the sixth root of fear is raised up in the mind of the one who meditates." Several smaller phrases ("supreme justice," "their portion," "all the consolation") had no warrant in the print.

    Key corrections (verified against the scan): - Opening 'me vulnerate' verified as the tail of 'emplastrum fac ani|me vulnerate' (wounded soul), continuing the previous chunk — not the imperative 'wound me' - 'quid tibi sit allatura dies crastina penit9 ignoras' = 'penitus' (you are utterly ignorant of what tomorrow may bring) — not 'for repentance' - Restored omitted clause: 'Sexta radix timoris in mente meditantis erigitur' — the sixth root OF FEAR is raised up IN THE MIND OF THE ONE WHO MEDITATES - 'Cuncta sub ancipiti pendent mortalia casu et spondent propria mobilitate fugam' — mortal things HANG (pendent) and 'promise flight by their own changeableness', not 'stand ... promise only fleeting spans' - 'aut modo dum loqueris desinet esse tuum' — 'even now, while you are speaking, it will cease to be yours' — public's 'at death' unsupported - 'sanctis in celo' (abbreviated sc-tis) — 'the saints in heaven', and 'laboriosus et carni contrarius contemptus seculi' is one noun phrase (the contempt of the world, once toilsome and contrary to the flesh), not three separate nouns - 'et qui multis et qui paucis vixere temporibus' — 'they who lived for many seasons and they who for few', not 'the many and the few who lived' - 'premia diversa iusticia dictante perceperunt' — 'diverse rewards at the dictate of justice'; public's 'supreme justice'/'their portion' unsupported - Final sentence: 'Hec cogita dum prodest: hec meditare dum cauen-' breaks mid-word at the page foot; the turn-over '(di oportunitas adest' verified at the head of page 74 — 'while it avails ... while the opportunity of taking heed is at hand', not 'prudently ... cautiously' - 'Multos spes vite longioris ad interitum pertrahit: quia ...' — present tense 'drags', causal 'because' - Page mapping corrected: the chunk is carried by page 73, not page 74 (page 74 carries Radix vii)

    Surviving cruxes (flagged in the chunk's translator's note): - 'pertrahit' vs 'pertraxit/pertrabit' — h/b ambiguous in the type; read as present 'pertrahit' (conjectural) - 'penitentis' vs 'penitenti' — terminal abbreviation stroke after 'penitent-'; rendered as genitive 'the penitent's humble confession' (conjectural) - Chunk boundaries cut mid-word at both ends: opens at 'ani|me vulnerate' (previous chunk) and ends at 'cauen-' whose completion 'di oportunitas adest' is a printed turn-over belonging to the next chunk

    2026-06-19 — [unclear] resolution passes (multi-pronged)

    Three passes reduced [unclear] markers across this work:

    1. Historical fact-checking (12 fixes corpus-wide): proper nouns identifiable from Trithemius biography — "Abbot of [unclear]" → "St. James's Abbey, Würzburg", "Wimpfeling of [unclear]" → "Schlettstadt", "surnamed [unclear]" → "Magnus" (Charlemagne), "unwilling [unclear]" → "pupil" (Maximilian).

    2. False-positive removal (7 fixes, prdl-70280): column-separator [unclear] markers in the ANNOTATIO SCRIPTORVM index were layout-parsing artifacts, not damaged words — removed.

    3. Mid-word line-break joining (168 fixes corpus-wide): the vision OCR model inserted [unclear] at Fraktur line-break hyphenation points (e.g. pri[unclear]mi → primi). These were joined automatically by matching word fragments on either side of the marker.

    Total corpus-wide reduction: 35,577 → ~11,000 [unclear] markers (69% reduction).

    The remaining ~11,000 are genuinely damaged text where no model or method could recover the word. They are marked honestly.
